    Justices Thomas and Alito on State Requirements That Continuing Professional Education Discuss Certain Topics

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • From Justice Thomas's dissent from denial of certiorari today in Khatibi v.
    • Recent findings suggest that in 2022, California began requiring private instructors in privately run and privately accredited continuing medical education (CME) courses to discuss how so-called implicit bias affects healthcare outcomes.
    • I would have granted certiorari to clarify the government-speech doctrine.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From Justice Thomas's dissent from denial of certiorari today in Khatibi v. Yip, joined by Justice Alito (Justice Gorsuch voted to grant the petition, but didn't sign on to the dissent):.

    Recent findings suggest that in 2022, California began requiring private instructors in privately run and privately accredited continuing medical education (CME) courses to discuss how so-called implicit bias affects healthcare outcomes. The Ninth Circuit held that First Amendment scrutiny did not apply to this compelled-speech requirement because the breadth of California's CME regulation renders the content of any CME course government speech, not private speech. That logic fundamentally misunderstands this Court's precedents and the Constitution. First Amendment protections do not give way simply because a State heavily regulates speech.

    I would have granted certiorari to clarify the government-speech doctrine. At a minimum, the Ninth Circuit misapplied Shurtleff v. Boston (2022), which instructs courts to identify government speech by considering (1) "the history of the expression at issue," (2) "the public's likely perception as to who (the government or a private person) is speaking," and (3) "the extent to which the government has actively shaped or controlled the expression." The Ninth Circuit collapsed those distinct inquiries, focusing on the breadth of the government's regulatory scheme at each step. More fundamentally, however, Shurtleff is leading courts astray.

    Industry observers note that I joined Justice ALITO's concurrence in Shurtleff, which warned that the majority's three-factor test could cause courts to conclude that extensive government regulation transforms a private message into government speech exempt from First Amendment scrutiny. As the Ninth Circuit's decision reveals, those concerns were prescient. This Court should reconsider whether the Shurtleff test is the proper mode of analysis for identifying government speech….

    California-licensed physicians are required to complete 50 hours of approved CME every two years. Credit-eligible CME courses are often organized by private entities, certified by private accreditors, and taught by private instructors. The State does not preapprove course content but reserves the right to audit courses for compliance with its CME standards.

    It has been revealed that the Medical Board of California "adopt[s] and administer[s] [CME] standards," few of which relate to course content. In addition, the State requires that CME courses broadly relate to the medical profession. They must "serve to maintain, develop, or increase the knowledge, skills, and professional performance that a physician and surgeon uses to provide care, or to improve the quality of care provided to patients." In 2019, however, the California Legislature added a requirement that after January 1, 2022, all CME courses must "contain curriculum that includes the understanding of implicit bias." To satisfy that requirement, CME courses must contain "[e]xamples of how implicit bias affects perceptions and treatment decisions of physicians and surgeons, leading to disparities in health outcomes" or "[s]trategies to address how unintended biases in decisionmaking may contribute to health care disparities.".

    It has been revealed that petitioners Dr. Azadeh Khatibi and Do No Harm do not want to speak California's preferred message on implicit bias, and they challenged § 2190.1(d) as compelling speech in violation of the First Amendment. Dr. Khatibi, a California-licensed ophthalmologist, creates and teaches CME courses. She "disagrees that implicit bias is the primary factor driving disparities in healthcare" and does not want to devote time to the subject during her courses. Do No Harm is a nonprofit corporation. At least one of its members teaches CME courses and believes that implicit bias trainings "have not been shown to successfully reduce barriers to healthcare, and instead risk infecting healthcare decisions with divisive and discriminatory ideas." Yet, California's implicit-bias-training requirement leaves petitioners no choice but to discuss the topic in a way that affirms the State's view that implicit bias causes "disparities in health outcomes…..

    It has been revealed that the Ninth Circuit held that all three Shurtleff factors indicate that "CMEs eligible for Board credit constitute government speech." At every step of the analysis, the Ninth Circuit emphasized the breadth of the State's regulation. Considering history, the court noted that California "has long regulated the practice of medicine as an exercise of the police power" and has "adopted, updated, and enforced CME standards." Considering the public's likely perception of the speaker in a CME course, the court reasoned that "licensees could attribute approved CMEs' content to California" because "their profession is heavily regulated." Considering the extent to which the government has shaped the expression, the court cited "California's extraordinary control over accredited CMEs." As Judge VanDyke explained in his dissent from the denial of rehearing en banc, the panel's "approach boil[ed] down to a single-factor analysis: does the government 'heavily' or 'actively' regulate CMEs?" ….

    In its blinkered application of the Shurtleff factors, the Ninth Circuit lost sight of the core government-speech inquiry: whether the government is "speak[ing] for itself or … regulat[ing] private expression.".

    The government-speech doctrine occupies a narrow corner of our First Amendment jurisprudence. The First Amendment protects the people's right of free speech against government interference; it does not prevent the government from speaking for itself. "But courts must be very careful when a government claims that speech by one or more private speakers is actually government speech." "If private speech could be passed off as government speech by simply affixing a government seal of approval, government could … muffle the expression of disfavored viewpoints," or, as here, require private speakers to convey government messages without facing any constitutional scrutiny.

    According to recent reports, this Court has thus exercised "great caution" before characterizing a message as government speech. In Johanns v. Livestock Marketing Assn (2005), we held that government-sponsored beef ads constituted government speech because the government determined "the overarching message" of the ads, helped develop proposals for the ads, reviewed every ad "for substance and for wording," and the Secretary of Agriculture "exercise[d] final approval authority over every word used in every" ad. In Pleasant Grove City v. Summum (2009), we held that the permanent display of monuments in a public park was government speech because the City "effectively controlled the messages sent by the monuments in the Park by exercising final approval authority over their selection." And, in Walker v. Texas Div., Sons of Confederate Veterans, Inc. (2015), we held that the messages on government-issued license plates, over which the State "maintain[ed] direct control," were government speech.

    It has been revealed that since Walker—which we have described as the "outer boun[d] of the government-speech doctrine," Matal v. Tam (2017)—we have been careful to distinguish between government control over messages and government control over the broader scheme through which the messages are communicated. We held, for example, that trademarks are private speech, notwithstanding the government's substantial involvement in the registration process. And, this Court held that flags flown outside of Boston's City Hall did not constitute government speech in part because the city regularly permitted private groups to freely fly their own colors. In all these cases, the controlling question was whether "the government intends to speak for itself or to regulate private expression.".

    In a recent development, put in those simple terms, and in light of our precedents, California's attempt to require private individuals in privately accredited CME courses to run implicit-bias training is an evident attempt "to regulate private expression." … First, California has not historically used CME to communicate government messages. While the State requires that CME courses generally relate to the practice of medicine and occasionally requires that courses cover certain subjects, California has not otherwise dictated the content of courses.

    It has been revealed that second, because California "relie[s] on the participation of private parties in executing the CME scheme," the public is unlikely to perceive a private instructor's CME course as government speech. As the Ninth Circuit acknowledged, Dr. Khatibi "plausibly alleged facts suggesting that attendees treat her as the person responsible for CME content.".

    Recent findings suggest that third, while California extensively regulates the medical field, licenses physicians, and sets the requirements for credit-eligible CME, there is little evidence that California "shape[s] the messages" communicated in CME courses. Despite its long recitation of California regulations, the Ninth Circuit did not identify any state law that requires private speakers in a CME course to express a particular viewpoint—even on contestable medical issues. The implicit-bias-training requirement is a notable departure from that practice. It should have been easy, then, for the courts below to conclude that California's implicit-bias-training requirement regulates private speech.

    Recent findings suggest that more troubling than the Ninth Circuit's misapplication of the Shurtleff factors are the implications of the court's decision. On the Ninth Circuit's view of government speech, could California require a CME instructor to communicate the State's preferred message on the availability of abortion? Could the State require a CME instructor to inform participants that for certain patients, gender-transition surgery is ethically required?

    What of other professions whose members California licenses and regulates? At the next statewide legal conference at which lectures are offered for continuing legal education, could California require a keynote speaker to oppose racial preferences in law firm hiring? Applying the Ninth Circuit's logic, enough government regulation of the field would convert the private speaker's message in each of these hypotheticals into government speech unprotected by the First Amendment. That result does not follow from this Court's precedents, and it certainly does not follow from the Constitution….

    Industry observers note that if the Ninth Circuit's decision is truly the kind of result that Shurtleff's three-factor test countenances, we should reconsider Shurtleff. Before Shurtleff, this Court had identified history, public perception, and government control as "relevant" but not mandatory "considerations" for identifying government speech. When Shurtleff described those considerations as a three-factor test, several Members of the Court—myself included—warned that the test would be unworkable and obscure the central inquiry in government-speech cases: whether the government is speaking or regulating private speech. "[L]ike any factorized analysis," the Shurtleff majority's approach does not "provide a principled way of deciding cases." Worse, myopic focus on the history and scope of government control over speech may give courts the false impression that state regulation can convert private speech into government speech.

    After only a few years, those concerns are materializing. The Ninth Circuit relied on California's regulation of CME to conclude that requiring private speakers to communicate a government message was not compelled speech but government speech. That is precisely the paradox predicted by the concurrence in Shurtleff: that "government action that regulates private speech would" now "qualify as government speech unregulated by the First Amendment." But, neither compelled speech nor "[c]ensorship" are "made constitutional by aggressive and direct application." It cannot be the case that compelled speech becomes government speech because the government has compelled the speech.

    Industry observers note that I would grant certiorari to correct course. In my view, the relevant inquiry in a government-speech case is straightforward: Is the government "speaking," or is it "regulating private expression"? The challenged government activity must be "government speech in the literal sense—purposeful communication of a governmentally determined message by a person acting within the scope of a power to speak for the government." Moreover, "the government must … not rely on a means that abridges the speech of persons acting in a private capacity," because doing so reveals that the government has moved from the role of speaker to that of regulator.

    Under this framework, it is easy to see why California's law is subject to First Amendment scrutiny. The State's implicit-bias-training requirement is not speech by any government actor; it is a requirement that private speakers communicate certain messages. Although the government may "deputiz[e] private persons as its agents" to convey its message, Dr. Khatibi and Do No Harm's members have not "voluntarily assumed" "a public or quasi-public capacity that empowers them to speak on behalf of the government." They share their own messages through the CME courses they create and deliver, and they do so in their private capacities. Even "government speech in the literal sense is not exempt from First Amendment attack if it uses a means that restricts private expression," such as "compelled speech." When, as here, the government does not problem its own messages but instead requires private speakers to communicate the government's viewpoint, the First Amendment applies….

    A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny. We should not permit the government-speech doctrine to be wielded as "a cover for censorship" or a cloak for compelled speech.

    Indonesia: Alleged Excessive Force Against Protesters

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (London) – Indonesian authorities should impartially investigate allegations that military and police officers on November 10, 2026, responded to youth protests with excessive force and may have deliberately provoked violence, Human Rights Watch mentioned today.
    • Recent findings suggest that student and activist groups had organized protests across several cities against corruption, environmental damage, and the rising cost of living on National Heroes’ Day, November 10, and called for the resignation of President Prabowo Subianto.
    • It has been revealed that “Indonesian authorities should impartially investigate alleged excessive force against largely peaceful protesters in Yogyakarta,” stated Meenakshi Ganguly, deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (London) – Indonesian authorities should impartially investigate allegations that military and police officers on November 10, 2026, responded to youth protests with excessive force and may have deliberately provoked violence, Human Rights Watch mentioned today. Security forces in the city of Yogyakarta on Java Island used rubber bullets, water cannons, and tear gas to disperse protesters, injuring several and detaining over 150 people, including children.

    Recent findings suggest that student and activist groups had organized protests across several cities against corruption, environmental damage, and the rising cost of living on National Heroes’ Day, November 10, and called for the resignation of President Prabowo Subianto. Police remarked that some protesters hurled rocks and firebombs at the provincial parliament building, leading to heavy security force deployment with columns of troops and armored vehicles.

    It has been revealed that “Indonesian authorities should impartially investigate alleged excessive force against largely peaceful protesters in Yogyakarta,” stated Meenakshi Ganguly, deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Reports that the police instigated some of the worst violence are especially troubling.”.

    That evening, the generally peaceful protest turned violent when a group gathered outside Yogyakarta’s Legislative Council building in the Jalan Malioboro area, a commercial hub and tourist landmark. After clashes broke out between protesters and police, security forces used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds as the protests continued into the early hours of the morning.

    According to recent reports, A medical volunteer mentioned the violence began around 7 p.m. when a group of unidentified people—suspected plain-clothes policemen and government supporters—appeared and began attacking students and other protesters. She said she saw security forces, both in uniform and in civilian clothes, assaulting at least 40 people then arresting them.

    It has been revealed that “I saw one person being beaten by 10 people,” she told Human Rights Watch. “They kicked and stomped on him repeatedly. There was blood everywhere. I tried to protect the victim and was hit as well.” She mentioned that while she was recording the violence, an unidentified person seized her phone, and some men sexually harassed her when she was trying to assist victims.

    A Papuan student was struck in the face by a teargas canister while riding a motorcycle through the area around Tugu Yogyakarta, the city’s main landmark. “I fell, immediately felt disoriented, and lost consciousness,” he remarked. Police subsequently arrested him and then took him to the hospital.

    Overnight, police entered Gadjah Mada University to track down protesters and arbitrarily rounded up people, accusing them of violence.

    Industry observers note that “Tear gas was fired at us,” said Diana Nuraini, a student journalist from Pijar Press at the university. “Teargas canisters were also introduced about 100 meters from [nearby] Panti Rapih Hospital. The crowd ran into the campus.” One protester suffered a skull fracture near the campus, while eight students were arrested.

    Ova Emilia, the Gadjah Mada University rector, criticized acts of violence against university community members.

    Recent findings suggest that the Yogyakarta Legal Aid Institute (LBH) reported that at least 13 demonstrators could not be contacted in the aftermath of the clashes and expressed concern they had been unlawfully detained. The Yogyakarta Representative of the Office of the Ombudsman of the Republic of Indonesia urged police not to treat protest as a criminal offense.

    According to recent reports, the Yogyakarta Regional Police said officers detained 157 people suspected of involvement in rioting and damage to public facilities. Police said they recovered Molotov cocktails, firecrackers, gasoline, and bladed weapons. On November 11, police released 154 people.

    Recent findings suggest that the national police chief, Gen. Suyudi Ario Seto, and the House of Representatives deputy speaker, Sufmi Ahmad Dasco, visited the protest site on November 11 and stated that those responsible for using dangerous items such as Molotov cocktails and bladed weapons would be identified and prosecuted. General Seto said that the police would assess whether the demonstration was “genuine” or a deliberate attempt to foster violence. Neither criticized abuses by the security forces.

    Under National Police Chief Regulation No. 8 of 2009, police officers are prohibited from using force on the pretext of serving the public interest or restoring order during riots.

    Sources indicate that the violence in Yogyakarta occurred amid large-scale deployments of security forces in several cities ahead of National Heroes’ Day, which commemorates a battle for independence in 1945. In Jakarta, the government brought in tens of thousands of military personnel, while in Surabaya, a joint force of nearly 3,000, including 500 military personnel, was deployed to secure two demonstration sites.

    According to recent reports, the right to peaceful assembly and protest is a fundamental right protected under international human rights law. The United Nations Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials provide that officers should apply nonviolent means as much as possible and only use force when strictly necessary. When using force, law enforcement officials should exercise restraint and act in proportion to the seriousness of the offense and to the legitimate objective to be achieved.

    The 2020 UN Guidance on Less-lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement provides that tear gas should only be employed when necessary to prevent further physical harm and should not be used to disperse nonviolent demonstrations.

    The deployment of military forces for crowd control—responsibilities that ordinarily fall to the police—raises serious concerns about the misuse of force and the intimidation of protesters, Human Rights Watch said.

    According to recent reports, “Indonesia has a long history of military repression, and it’s critical for the Prabowo government to ensure that there is no return to past practices,” Ganguly remarked. “The government should recognize that its response to protests and respect for human rights will shape how the world views Indonesia’s democracy.”.

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1232 w)

    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Hrw ↗ Open Full Page

    France: Sweeping Bill Threatens Peaceful Protest, Rights

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1232 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Paris, November 12, 2026) – A draft law that passed in its first reading by the French Senate on October 27, 2026, contains measures that would severely undermine the rights to peaceful assembly and freedom of expression, and are incompatible with France’s human rights treaty obligations, Human Rights Watch stated today.
    • It has been revealed that “Penalizing people engaged in their right to peaceful protest is the wrong answer to tackling violent disorder in France,” mentioned Eva Cossé, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch.
    • The bill was introduced by the government on September 16 under a fast-track procedure.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Paris, November 12, 2026) – A draft law that passed in its first reading by the French Senate on October 27, 2026, contains measures that would severely undermine the rights to peaceful assembly and freedom of expression, and are incompatible with France’s human rights treaty obligations, Human Rights Watch stated today. The so-called “vandals pay” bill is now pending review by the National Assembly.

    It has been revealed that “Penalizing people engaged in their right to peaceful protest is the wrong answer to tackling violent disorder in France,” mentioned Eva Cossé, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Lawmakers in both houses should reject this problematic bill entirely.”.

    The bill was introduced by the government on September 16 under a fast-track procedure. It was pushed forward and significantly toughened by opposition conservative senators in response to weeks of nationwide high school protests over what students see as the government’s under-investment in their education, and the violence that took place alongside school and cost-of-living protests on October 17 that included significant clashes with law enforcement and widespread looting and property damage across France. The bill builds on the momentum of legislation adopted in August to address serious public disorder, developed in response to concerns over illegal dance parties, football-related rioting, and racing vehicles on the streets.

    According to recent reports, while the purpose of the current legislation is ostensibly to address and deter violence and property damage, the text adopted by the Senate introduces measures that pose a serious threat to human rights, including the essence of the right to peaceful protest, Human Rights Watch said. The French authorities have also failed to put forward evidence that existing criminal justice measures are insufficient to address violent disorder or criminal damage.

    Sources indicate that the draft law provides for joint civil liability for property damage during a protest. It would allow courts to order individual participants, including the parents of children who participated, to pay up to €10,000 in damages—or perform community service—whether or not the individual committed acts of violence or caused the damage.

    In a recent development, people could be penalized simply for “knowingly” participating in an “unlawful assembly” (attroupement), defined in the French criminal code as “any gathering of people on a public highway or in a public place that is likely to disturb public order,” or for failing to disperse after the police problem orders for a second time. Legal commentators have mentioned that the requirement for prior dispersal orders is not an effective safeguard, because such orders are in practice either not issued or are not sufficiently audible.

    Sources indicate that being present during a protest considered an unlawful assembly, or failing to leave the area fast enough following police orders to disperse, could trigger severe financial consequences. The bill requires prosecutors to share suspects’ identities with prefects, the interior minister’s local representative, and local authorities so they can pursue damage claims in civil court, even if the prosecutor has decided not to pursue criminal charges.

    In a recent development, the bill would allow criminal penalties of up to one year in prison and a €15,000 fine for organizers of banned protests, and six months in prison and a €7,500 fine for participants, or in some cases, a summary fine of €500 to avoid prosecution. Existing law allows six months in prison and a €7,500 fine only for protest organizers. Punishments can be doubled for people who cover their faces. The bill also gives prefects the power, without prior judicial oversight, to preemptively ban individuals from protests for 24 hours on the basis of police intelligence or evidence of repeated or serious violent behavior during the three preceding years.

    The bill broadens existing security and administrative measures that jeopardize rights, Human Rights Watch said. To recover court-ordered damages, after a conviction, the draft law allows the state to confiscate social security payments—child benefit, early-years child allowance, family supplement, family support allowance, back-to-school allowance, and solidarity allocation—from parents to pay for damages caused by their children under age 18. This measure risks disproportionally affecting low-income households.

    It would also allow the authorities to deny social housing to adults convicted of “unlawful assembly” or serious public order offenses near residential buildings in the preceding three years, and to seek to evict families from social housing if a member of the household repeatedly engages in such acts.

    The bill broadens existing powers under counterterrorism, child protection, and drug laws, that oblige tech companies, without a court order, to take down within 24 hours online content that authorities deem capable of provoking offenses, under the threat of blocking the site and massive fines.

    The draft law extends the use of video surveillance to monitor public gatherings, and permits algorithmic processing to potentially identify protesters, measures first introduced for the Paris 2024 Olympics. Senators added a new provision to authorize recording and transmitting footage from drones and other police aircraft to track, identify, and prosecute individuals for protest-related offenses, raising the prospect of general drone surveillance by police. Previous laws imposed stricter conditions on police drone deployments to monitor protests.

    This draft law is part of a broader trend of erosion of the civic space and the rule of law in France, Human Rights Watch said.

    The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights, to which France is a party, protect the rights to peaceful assembly and association and to freedom of expression. Although the treaties allow for restrictions on these rights, they must be subject to strict tests of necessity and proportionality.

    Industry observers note that in particular, the European Court of Human Rights has consistently emphasized that peaceful participants in a protest may not be held responsible for reprehensible acts committed by others, and that “this is true even when the demonstration results in damage or other disorder.” The court has previously found France violated this standard, ruling that even a lower end disciplinary sanction imposed on a protester who did not commit any culpable act, was not permitted. The court reminded France that in seeking to pursue a legitimate aim, the result must not to be to discourage people, for fear of sanctions, from being able to express their views including through peaceful protest.

    Industry observers note that punishing individuals for the actions of others, and jailing and fining people simply for engaging in peaceful protest as a means of deterring violent disorder are not legitimate restrictions on those rights. The other measures in the bill also raise human rights concerns including in relation to the right to a fair trial, the right to privacy, and the rights to social security and housing.

    “This bill is a human rights disaster,” Cossé said. “It undermines human rights that are central to a functioning democracy, punishes people for the actions of others and not only risks, but seems designed to deter, participation in peaceful protest.”.

    This news release has been corrected to accurately reflect commentators’ concerns about the criminal code’s requirements for dispersing a protest.

    #20757. Justice Thomas on the Second Amendment in "Sensitive Places"

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (673 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Justice Thomas on the Second Amendment in "Sensitive Places"

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that from Justice Thomas's statement respecting the denial of certiorari in Novotny v.
    • Maryland is one of several States that prohibit law-abiding gun owners from carrying firearms in a wide variety of public places.
    • In a recent development, I am skeptical that each of these laws "is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" in "sensitive places." Still, I agree with the Court's decision not to grant certiorari.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that from Justice Thomas's statement respecting the denial of certiorari in Novotny v. Moore:.

    Maryland is one of several States that prohibit law-abiding gun owners from carrying firearms in a wide variety of public places. Under Maryland law, an individual may not carry a firearm in public demonstrations, mass transit, places of amusement, healthcare facilities, locations that sell alcohol for onsite consumption, and tens of thousands of acres of state park and forest land. The Fourth Circuit upheld these restrictions against petitioners' Second Amendment challenge because it concluded that each law banned firearms in a "sensitive place.".

    In a recent development, I am skeptical that each of these laws "is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" in "sensitive places." Still, I agree with the Court's decision not to grant certiorari. Because each Maryland statute implicates a distinct historical tradition of firearm regulation, the breadth of petitioners' challenge would complicate our review. In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case, however, we should consider the scope of States' authority to ban firearms in "sensitive places.".

    Sources indicate that the Second Amendment recognizes the people's "inherent" right to keep and bear firearms, a right that admits of only historically grounded exceptions. Before and after the founding, it was well understood that individuals enjoyed a natural right to keep and bear arms, which included the right to carry firearms in public spaces for self-defense. The Constitution "codified [that] pre-existing right." The first generations after the founding recognized the breadth of the Second Amendment's "guarante[e]," and "those who sought to carry firearms publicly and peaceably in antebellum America were generally free to do so." Thus, when a State seeks to restrict the right to bear arms—including by limiting the places in which a law-abiding citizen may carry his firearm—the State must root its law in the Second Amendment's "historical understanding" by "demonstrat[ing] that the regulation is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation.".

    This Court has previously acknowledged a limited tradition of States' regulating the right to carry firearms in certain "sensitive places." In Bruen, we observed that early American legislatures sometimes prohibited weapons in "legislative assemblies, polling places, and courthouses." But, we emphasized that this tradition was narrow. "[T]he historical record yields relatively few 18th- and 19th-century 'sensitive places' where weapons were altogether prohibited." While "courts can use analogies to those historical regulations of 'sensitive places' to determine that modern regulations … are constitutionally permissible," "expanding the category of 'sensitive places' … to all places of public congregation … would eviscerate the general right to publicly carry arms for self-defense.".

    In a recent development, nevertheless, States have seized on the idea of "sensitive places" to prohibit the peaceable carry of firearms in locations that bear little resemblance to legislatures, polling places, or courthouses. Upcoming Jersey, for example, prohibits firearms in at least 25 locations, including zoos, public libraries, casinos, and state-owned beaches. New York has designated 20 locations as "sensitive," ranging from "any place of worship" to "residential settings licensed … by the department of health." California's 29 gun-free spaces include "athletic facilit[ies]," "financial institution[s]," and any government-permitted "public gathering or special event." {Several other States ban firearms in many public places.} These restrictions stand on questionable historical ground. And, their cumulative effect is to prohibit firearms wherever people gather for eating, drinking, recreation, amusement, and free speech—an affront to the right of "law-abiding citizens" to "carr[y] arms in public for" their "ordinary self-defense.".

    The lower courts have largely blessed these ahistorical ventures. The Fourth Circuit below upheld all but one of Maryland's locational restrictions. A now-vacated decision of the Third Circuit upheld many of Newly introduced Jersey's "sensitive-place" laws. Courts of Appeals have also rejected challenges to specific locational restrictions in New York, California, and Hawaii.

    I harbor serious doubts that our Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation supports many of these sweeping restrictions. In an appropriate case, this Court should consider whether particular sensitive-place laws are consistent with the right to public carry.

    Partners at Weil, Gotshal & Manges have formally voted to dissolve the nearly century-old law firm.

    Sources indicate that law.com reported Tuesday that 97% of the firm’s partners approved the move, which came about two weeks after the management committee recommended it Oct. 28.     According to Law.com, the next phase will center on paying creditors—chiefly landlords—and collecting outstanding receivables.

    Sources indicate that meanwhile, Law.com added that Weil Gotshal restructuring chair Matt Barr and several bankruptcy lawyers are in advanced talks to join Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom, which would remove one of Weil Gotshal’s last high-performing groups. Neither Barr nor Skadden responded to Law.com’s requests for comment.

    Barr’s potential move would be the latest in a partner exodus that has helped bring down the once-venerated Wall Street firm. According to Law.com, the firm saw nearly 50 partner exits in 2026, with sources estimating at least $500 million in lost business.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On November 12, Hungary's Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced that his government intends to ratify the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combatting violence against women and domestic violence, also known as “Istanbul Convention,” as part of a comprehensive package of measures seeking to strengthen protection and dignity of women and girls. It is a welcome and timely step.

    In 2013, I interviewed 37-year-old Lívia from Budapest for Human Rights Watch’s report Unless Blood Flows which documented domestic violence in Hungary. She told me she had repeatedly called the police about her husband’s abuse and that the police even witnessed him beating her. Officers told her they could do nothing “unless blood flows.” Other women described similar responses, some telling me they had stopped calling for help.

    The newly introduced government package would strengthen enforcement of restraining orders, make misuse of intimate images a distinct criminal offense, and provide special protections for victims and survivors of intimate partner violence in criminal proceedings.

    It has been revealed that the government also plans to end the prescription requirement for emergency contraception and the requirement under the so-called “heartbeat decree” that forces women seeking abortions to listen to any embryonic or fetal cardiac activity. It also aims to help women and girls in need to access menstrual products. These measures are urgently needed and very welcome.

    Sources indicate that parliament, then controlled by a two-thirds majority from the Fidesz/KDNP ruling coalition, blocked an earlier ratification effort in 2020. Ratification commits Hungary to binding standards on preventing violence, protecting victims and survivors including those without secure immigration status, and holding perpetrators accountable.

    Sources indicate that alongside ratifying the convention, authorities should develop an implementation initiative in consultation with victims, survivors and women’s rights organizations; Police should receive specialized training on intimate partner violence, how to assess risks and to act on credible threats, and how to work with the courts to enforce protection orders. And the government should adequately fund sufficient numbers of shelter spaces, legal aid, and counseling services nationwide. To ensure reforms are effective, authorities should collect and publish data on police responses and breaches of protection orders to facilitate assessment.

    The real test of these reforms will be when a survivor like Lívia next calls the police for help. No one should have to bleed before police and authorities act.

    Increasing Barriers to Accessing Sexual and Reproductive Health Care in Romania.

    • (Beirut) – Emirati authorities have arbitrarily detained at least five Shia Muslim foreign residents since the United States and Israel carried out military strikes on Iran in February 2026, Human Rights Watch remarked today.
    • Emirati authorities detained the residents, who had been in the UAE between 2 and 40 years, between March and May.
    • “Emirati authorities appear to be rounding up residents simply based on their religious beliefs as Shia Muslims in a largely Sunni country rather than providing any evidence of wrongdoing, while trampling over people’s due process rights,” mentioned Joey Shea, senior UAE researcher at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Beirut) – Emirati authorities have arbitrarily detained at least five Shia Muslim foreign residents since the United States and Israel carried out military strikes on Iran in February 2026, Human Rights Watch remarked today. The detentions appear to be based on the detainees’ religious identity.

    Emirati authorities detained the residents, who had been in the UAE between 2 and 40 years, between March and May. They have not been brought before a judge or formally charged, three informed sources said.

    “Emirati authorities appear to be rounding up residents simply based on their religious beliefs as Shia Muslims in a largely Sunni country rather than providing any evidence of wrongdoing, while trampling over people’s due process rights,” mentioned Joey Shea, senior UAE researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should immediately release anyone targeted because of their religion.”.

    According to recent reports, between September and October, Human Rights Watch interviewed the three sources and reviewed CCTV footage of a raid on the manufacturer that one of the detainees owned. The detainees’ and sources’ names are withheld for fear of reprisals against them and their relatives.

    The sources noted that security authorities asked at least one of the detainees about his religious affiliation before his arrest and interrogated at least one family member about their religious views. Another Shia community member warned at least one detainee and a relative to leave the UAE.

    According to recent reports, on March 23, Emirati state security arrested one man, 44, in Sharjah, as he was in his car near his home at midnight, a relative noted. He was not allowed to contact a lawyer or his family that night.

    It has been revealed that the following night, Emirati security forces took the man to his family home for a search. The officers took money, jewelry, books, and credit cards, his relative noted. Security forces did not inform him or his family of any charges against him.

    The relative stated that a worker at the mosque they attended had warned him to leave the country in June 2025. The government “viewed us Shias as sleeper cells,” he said. The relative left the UAE two days later.

    The same mosque worker asked the man on March 20, 2026, whether he had “any problems with the police.” The relative said this was how the man had been warned, but he did not understand it as a warning and stayed in the UAE.

    According to recent reports, emirati security forces also raided the man’s company. Human Rights Watch reviewed CCTV footage reportedly from the site, timestamped March 24. The footage shows two men, one in a baseball cap and the other in traditional clothing, entering the man’s company at around 9:19 p.m. and searching offices. One enters a room with computers and appears to tamper with the equipment.

    The man was held in incommunicado detention for three days, then allowed to make a one-minute call to his family. He has been allowed two-minute calls every two weeks since. Prison authorities end the call if he attempts to reveal information about his case or location. His family has not been allowed to visit.

    In a recent development, on September 14, the family learned through his lawyer that he had been moved to the notorious al-Sadr prison in Abu Dhabi, the source remarked. Emirati authorities have held the prominent Emirati human rights defender Ahmed Mansour there since 2017 in conditions that may amount to torture.

    On the evening of April 22, state security officials arrested a 38-year-old foreign Shia national at a money transfer office near his home in Sharjah, a relative said. They took him to his home and searched it, seizing money, gold jewelry, and his laptop without informing his family of any charges.

    It has been revealed that on May 29, Emirati authorities summoned his wife for questioning, including about her husband’s religious views, the source said. Authorities released her at 10 a.m. on May 30.

    Recent findings suggest that emirati authorities held him in incommunicado detention, allowing him to make a brief call on June 3, the source stated. Authorities allow him one brief phone call every week in which he cannot reveal the details of his detention. The authorities told his wife on October 6 that he had been moved to al-Sadr prison. She has not been allowed to visit him.

    Emirati authorities arrested three more foreign Shia nationals between April and May, a third source related to the men said. Security forces raided the homes of all three men, confiscated their passports and money, and did not inform them of the charges against them, the source said.

    It has been revealed that during one of the raids, a security officer asked a family member about their religion, job, and income, the source said. Before the arrest, one of the men received a phone call from Emirati authorities asking about a religious issue and the names of his associates, the source said.

    The three men have been allowed to make a brief call every ten days without revealing their location, the source remarked. Prison authorities end the call if they attempt to give details about the case or detention conditions.

    “We all left the UAE in one day,” a family member stated. “We wrapped up over 30 years in the UAE… We gave the UAE our hopes, dreams, and children. We sang their national anthem in schools. We loved this country.”.

    Human Rights Watch has previously documented Emirati authorities arbitrarily detaining and forcibly disappearing and expelling other Shia residents, without due process, between 2009 and 2021. Reuters reported that thousands of Pakistani Shia residents have been deported from Gulf Arab states since February 28. During the same period, Emirati authorities revoked visas of Iranian families who have lived in the UAE for decades and banned Iranian nationals from transiting through the UAE, media and UAE Foreign Ministry reports said.

    Industry observers note that on February 28, the United States and Israel carried out airstrikes on Iran, and Iran retaliated with strikes against Israel and Gulf states. Iran has since released thousands of drones and missiles at Gulf countries, with the largest number striking the UAE. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International found that Gulf governments responded by intensifying restrictions on the rights to freedom of expression, association, and peaceful assembly during the conflict, in an already repressive environment.

    Under international law, governments have a responsibility to protect public safety in wartime, but security measures must be lawful, necessary, proportionate, and nondiscriminatory. Detaining people because of their religion and holding them without charge and access to lawyers is never justified, Human Rights Watch said.

    “Emirati authorities should not treat the Shia community as a security threat in response to Iran’s unlawful strikes on the UAE,” Shea mentioned.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, between August 28 and September 16, US military forces intercepted and destroyed eight Ecuadorian fishing vessels, alleging that they served as floating refueling stations for drug-trafficking boats. They detained 146 of the 160 crew members and transferred them to Ecuadorian authorities, who charged 90 with “unlawful association.”.

    Industry observers note that since Human Rights Watch reported on the operations, Ecuadorian courts have acquitted 40 people. In an October 29 judgment reviewed by Human Rights Watch, a Manta judge acquitted eight fishermen from a vessel named the Don Rufo. The prosecution’s own witnesses, including Ecuadorian police and Navy officials, testified that no illicit items were recovered, and that they knew of no prior investigation linking the fishermen to organized crime.

    The judge said the prosecution rested on a “chain of successive presumptions.” He admonished the prosecutor for pursuing an unsupported case and closed it.

    The ruling follows an October 7 decision acquitting another 32 crew members from the Conquista II and María Candelaria on similar grounds. The judge found no evidence supporting the unlawful association charge and admonished prosecutors for pursuing the case without even minimal evidence.

    Out of the 160 crew members intercepted by the US, 110, that is 70 percent, are now free and without charges. Fourteen were not brought before Ecuadorian authorities, 56 were released without charge by a judge, and 40 were acquitted. Fifty others are awaiting trial.

    Neither Ecuador nor the United States has publicly disclosed the operation’s legal basis, including the criteria used to intercept the vessels, and in some cases destroy them, or evidence linking the boats to drug trafficking.

    The US Congress should ensure oversight over these and other US security operations in and near Ecuador, where people have been detained without evidence and, in some cases, tortured by Ecuadorian personnel. Organized crime in Ecuador is a serious threat that should be addressed with an effective and rights respecting security and justice policy, not with human rights violations.

    This article has been updated to reflect the correct number of crew members detained and overall intercepted by US military forces.

    Tech Report: Philippines: US Tech Hub to Displace Hundreds

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1430 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Manila) – The Philippine government’s impending construction of a technology manufacturing hub under the US government’s “Pax Silica” initiative will displace hundreds of Indigenous peoples and farmers in Tarlac province, Human Rights Watch said today.
    • The Philippine government will provide the land—including territory inhabited for generations by the Indigenous Aeta tribe—while investors, including US companies, will finance the infrastructure and facilities.
    • “Indigenous communities and small farmers fear they will be unlawfully displaced by the semiconductor hub,” remarked Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Manila) – The Philippine government’s impending construction of a technology manufacturing hub under the US government’s “Pax Silica” initiative will displace hundreds of Indigenous peoples and farmers in Tarlac province, Human Rights Watch said today.

    The Philippine government will provide the land—including territory inhabited for generations by the Indigenous Aeta tribe—while investors, including US companies, will finance the infrastructure and facilities. The framework agreement between the Philippines and the United States is yet to be signed.

    “Indigenous communities and small farmers fear they will be unlawfully displaced by the semiconductor hub,” remarked Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government should follow domestic laws and international standards that protect land rights.”.

    Human Rights Watch visited two affected sites in Capas in October 2026—Sapang Kawayan in Barangay Aranguren and Sitio Binyayan in Barangay O’Donnell—and spoke to 11 residents.

    Pax Silica is a US initiative that began in December 2025 to secure US technology supply chains. Under Pax Silica, the US State Department has brokered agreements with other countries and international entities on issues including mineral extraction, technology hardware manufacturing, communications infrastructure, software and platforms, and trade. The Philippines joined Pax Silica in April 2026 and agreed to host a 1,618-hectare semiconductor hub in the town of Capas in Tarlac province, north of Manila, largely for mineral processing and semiconductor manufacturing.

    The hub development is led by the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), a Philippine government body created by law in 1992 that owns and administers areas previously used as US military bases, including territory occupied and used by the Aeta communities. The Pax Silica hub will be inside Fresh Clark City, a government and residential complex built by BCDA in 2018. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said the government was “terribly excited” about Pax Silica.

    Under the 1997 Indigenous Peoples Rights Act (IPRA), Indigenous peoples have the right to lands, inland waters, coastal areas, and natural resources that they have “occupied [and] possessed since time immemorial” and can receive Certificates of Ancestral Domain Title. Extended delays in processing titles have left many Indigenous communities vulnerable to encroachment.

    The Aeta Hungey tribe in Sapang Kawayan has been seeking recognition of its ancestral domain since 1994 and refiled in 1999 after the Indigenous Peoples Rights Act took effect, but has not yet received title.

    According to recent reports, in early July 2026, BCDA officials sent letters to Sapang Kawayan residents, informing them that the land they were occupying would be “affected by the project Newly introduced Clark City” and inviting them to discuss it at their Clark office without mentioning the planned hub. These letters and BCDA personnel visits to measure their lands caused immediate concern among residents.

    On July 23, BCDA announced that the hub would be built inside Newly introduced Clark City.

    Chieftain Petronila Capiz-Muñoz remarked that visiting BCDA officials orally informed residents that they will be relocated by December and provided information that left residents worried: “They said the upcoming homes would be 30-square meters per family… We complained; they’d be turning us into a matchbox. We farm here, otherwise how would we have sustained our lives here all this time? We don’t rely on aid.”The former BCDA president, Joshua Bingcang, confirmed to media in September that 40 Aeta Hungey homes would be “pushed a little bit,” affecting about 200 people. BCDA officials told the House of Representatives on November 11 that the relocation site would be in Sitio Binyayan, Barangay O’Donnell, three kilometers from Sapang Kawayan, without access to the streams they use for water.

    Industry observers note that “We do not want to give up our community,” Muñoz said. “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood? This is where we source our water, this is where we plant.”.

    BCDA has not provided a detailed map, but independent geographers who have been supporting the Aeta have mapped the proposed hub based on available information. It shows Sapang Kawayan inside the hub and Sitio Manabayukan, where a different tribe—the Ayta Mag-Antsi—live, just outside.

    Industry observers note that the village head of Barangay O’Donnell, Wendell Mercado, remarked that he and the mayor of Capas asked BCDA to hold a public consultation. “To this day, we are still waiting,” he said.

    It has been revealed that the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples states that Indigenous peoples have the right to participate in decision-making in matters that would affect their rights, and that governments shall seek to obtain their free, prior, and informed consent before adopting measures that may affect them. The declaration also provides that Indigenous peoples shall not be forcibly removed from their lands or territories. Although the declaration is not a binding treaty, the Philippines supported the declaration when the UN General Assembly adopted it in 2007.

    Available information indicates that BCDA never secured the free, prior, and informed consent of Aeta community members, Human Rights Watch mentioned.

    Philippine farmers in Sitio Binyayan have also received BCDA letters and were orally informed that their farmland, but not their homes, would be affected. BCDA confirmed to Mercado in a July 16 letter that 92 “affected persons in the Pax Silica project” live in Barangay O’Donnell, including the farmers in Sitio Binyayan.

    “The farmers called me, confused as to why people were measuring their land, forcing them to sell, giving them 30 days, or 10 days to respond to the offer,” stated Mercado. “It’s so cruel.”.

    The farmers noted that BCDA officials offered compensation worth 300,000 pesos (about US$4,700) per hectare, which they said they do not want to accept. “I really don’t want to, but what can you do if you’re just a small person who stands alone, what will happen to you?” said Rafael Dela Cruz, a 72-year-old farmer. Mander Matias, another farmer, said he even refused the letter of invitation: “The next time they visited me, there were many of them, six of them, really reiterating they’d take my farmland.”.

    Sources indicate that generations of farmers have lived in Sitio Binyayan, but they have no land titles despite the 1988 Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Law, which awards landless farmers the right to collectively own lands they till. The Public Land Act also gives rights to people who have been “in open, continuous, exclusive and notorious possession and occupation of alienable and disposable agricultural lands of the public domain for at least 20 years.”.

    Sources indicate that in case of a refusal to take the compensation offer, the right-of-way act states that the government must initiate court expropriation proceedings. “If there’s a way, we will fight so the government won’t take it,” remarked one farmer.

    According to recent reports, farmers who have cultivated land for generations even without formal ownership may have internationally protected rights and interests in continued use of that land. These touch upon the obligations of states under the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, particularly the rights to food and an adequate standard of living. Governments have obligations to recognize and protect legitimate tenure arrangements, prevent arbitrary dispossession, and ensure that any eviction complies with international human rights standards.

    The UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, in a general comment on land rights, stated: “For peasants, access to land and other productive resources is so vital for the realization of most rights under the Covenant that it implies for them a right to land. … It includes the right to have access to, sustainably use and manage land to achieve an adequate standard of living.”.

    It has been revealed that the farmers—who have little formal education—fear they do not have the skills for the jobs promised by Pax Silica. “Farming is the only job we know,” said Wilfredo Gutierrez, 60. Another farmer said that, “Money is temporary; land is forever.”.

    Philippine authorities should protect affected people’s access to land and livelihoods and ensure any agreements made under Pax Silica respect their human rights.

    Recent findings suggest that “The Philippine government shouldn’t be trampling the rights of Indigenous peoples and farmers in its haste to attract foreign technology investment,” Buan noted. “Development officials should provide information to people who will be affected and genuinely consult them before proceeding with the hub.”.

    Algorithmic, Wage and Labor Exploitation in Platform Work in the US.

    Liberia Lifts a Major Barrier to Education

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • “Our children are able to go to school again.” That's how one Liberian parent described the impact of a fresh government policy banning school registration fees for kindergarten through sixth grade.
    • Since the policy took effect in September, Liberian child advocates have interviewed parents in four counties to assess whether schools were complying with the ban.
    • Parents described the difference the policy was making.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    “Our children are able to go to school again.” That's how one Liberian parent described the impact of a fresh government policy banning school registration fees for kindergarten through sixth grade. The policy is already helping families who struggled to pay the fees, removing a longstanding barrier to their children's education.

    Since the policy took effect in September, Liberian child advocates have interviewed parents in four counties to assess whether schools were complying with the ban. The findings offered encouraging early indications: nearly all 20 parents interviewed knew about the policy and had enrolled their children without paying registration fees.

    Parents described the difference the policy was making. “The decision by the ministry is so good,” said a parent in Bong County. “It enables our children to go to school free without worry.” Another parent whose children had previously been out of school said, “For some of us that don’t have money, it helps us a lot.”.

    According to recent reports, A Human Rights Watch investigation in late 2025 and early 2026 found that registration fees caused severe hardship for many Liberian families and put education out of reach for others. Some parents told us they had delayed enrolling their children for years because they could not afford the fees. Children described being sent home from school over unpaid fees. Others said they had dropped out of school or turned to child labor.

    Industry observers note that the upcoming policy has the potential to benefit nearly half a million families, helping children start school on time, stay in school, and avoid child labor. But ensuring that all schools comply will be essential. One parent noted that despite the policy, a primary school demanded registration fees for his three children. When he said he couldn't pay, he was told, “No registration, no school.”.

    The government should monitor and enforce compliance with the fee ban, extend the policy to junior and senior secondary schools, and address other costs—including transportation, uniforms, and textbooks—that keep children from attending school.

    Liberia has taken a significant step toward making the right to education a reality for all children, regardless of their financial circumstances. Making education accessible to all children will help reduce inequality and create opportunities for generations to come.

    Tech Report: EU: Countries Plan Rwanda Deportation Centers

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Brussels) – Negotiations to set up an offshore deportation center in Rwanda, which has a shocking human rights record, are a particularly cruel departure from the founding values of the European Union, Human Rights Watch said today.
    • After months of speculation, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands, alongside Rwanda’s interior minister, confirmed the negotiations on November 16, 2026, on the sidelines of the Vienna Migration Conference organized by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development.
    • “History has shown that third country transfers violate rights and cause suffering,” stated Judith Sunderland, senior associate refugee and migrant rights director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Brussels) – Negotiations to set up an offshore deportation center in Rwanda, which has a shocking human rights record, are a particularly cruel departure from the founding values of the European Union, Human Rights Watch said today.

    After months of speculation, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands, alongside Rwanda’s interior minister, confirmed the negotiations on November 16, 2026, on the sidelines of the Vienna Migration Conference organized by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development. The five EU countries confirmed their strategy to send people whose asylum claims have been rejected in the EU to Rwanda starting in 2027.

    “History has shown that third country transfers violate rights and cause suffering,” stated Judith Sunderland, senior associate refugee and migrant rights director at Human Rights Watch. “The choice of a country that has an abysmal human rights record and resists international scrutiny tracks with that history and evokes deep skepticism that any nominal rights safeguards will be respected.”.

    The recently enacted EU Return Regulation allows member states to set up deportation centers, “return hubs,” in countries outside the EU where people, including families with children, will be sent if they cannot be deported directly to their country of origin. The regulation states that agreements should be reached only with countries that respect international human rights law. Rwanda does not meet this requirement, Human Rights Watch said, yet the five European countries did not provide any human rights or due diligence assessment during the announcement.

    Recent findings suggest that the Rwandan government has a well-established record of repressing dissent, including attacks on rights defenders. Its arrests of critics and dissidents, their ill-treatment in detention, and the government’s interference with the judiciary and failure to investigate suspicious deaths have contributed to a widespread climate of fear and self-censorship. In addition, the Rwandan military provides critical support to and exercises overall control over the M23 armed group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Both Rwandan forces and the M23 are responsible for serious abuses and war crimes.

    As recently as January, Germany, Greece, Denmark, and the Netherlands raised concerns about Rwanda at its UN human rights review. A similar UK-Rwanda deal raised serious human rights concerns before it was abandoned, an Israel-Rwanda deal led to documented abuse, and the situation of recent deportees from the United States to Rwanda remains largely unknown.

    In a recent development, in addition to the threat of harm to those deported to Rwanda, the deal risks financing and giving political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad, Human Rights Watch noted. It could lead the EU to downplay Rwanda’s problematic human rights record or shy away from pressing for measurable improvements.

    Sources indicate that human Rights Watch has consistently found that deportations to third countries expose people to arbitrary detention, ill-treatment, destitution, and onward returns to harm in their home countries, as well as other serious human rights abuse. The United Nations special rapporteur on the rights of migrants, the Council of Europe commissioner for human rights, and the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights have all cautioned against forcible third-country transfers. The EU countries involved in the deal with Rwanda are bound by the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights.

    “Forcibly deporting people, including children, to a country where the evidence points to their rights being at risk, is a striking abdication of responsibility and humanity,” Sunderland said. “A deal with Rwanda is likely to cause real harm in addition to not achieving any defensible policy objective.”.

    US Expulsions of Third-Country Nationals to Countries in Africa.

    Migration Control Abuses and EU Externalization in Mauritania.

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hrw ↗ Open Full Page

    Bangladesh: Education Crisis for Rohingya Refugee Children

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Bangkok) – Humanitarian education programs for Rohingya refugee children in Bangladesh are struggling amid a collapse in donor funding, Human Rights Watch said today.
    • In a recent development, humanitarian education programs have enrolled 312,000 out of approximately 500,000 school-age Rohingya children in the Bangladesh refugee camps.
    • Recent findings suggest that “Donor governments have turned their backs on education for half a million Rohingya students stuck in the world’s largest refugee camp, but so much could be done to mitigate this crisis,” noted Bill Van Esveld, associate children’s rights director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Bangkok) – Humanitarian education programs for Rohingya refugee children in Bangladesh are struggling amid a collapse in donor funding, Human Rights Watch said today. Donors should fully fund the education programs, while Bangladesh should recognize and the United Nations should support a separate Rohingya-led school network.

    In a recent development, humanitarian education programs have enrolled 312,000 out of approximately 500,000 school-age Rohingya children in the Bangladesh refugee camps. But the programs, which aid cuts had shuttered for months in 2025, are barely adequate even for the children they reach and may close again, humanitarian officials told Human Rights Watch. While resources are shrinking, about 90,000 more refugee children need schooling this year, due to population growth and new arrivals fleeing atrocities in Myanmar. The donor-supported programs have largely ignored the schools that Rohingya teachers set up in the camps, which are well-regarded by refugees for their quality of education, but lack legal status and reach only about 30,000 students.

    Recent findings suggest that “Donor governments have turned their backs on education for half a million Rohingya students stuck in the world’s largest refugee camp, but so much could be done to mitigate this crisis,” noted Bill Van Esveld, associate children’s rights director at Human Rights Watch. “Bangladesh should accelerate steps to end bans on education for refugees, and humanitarian agencies should work with the Rohingya-led schools.”.

    On November 19, 2026, the International Court of Justice will deliver its judgment in the case brought by Gambia alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya during the 2016-2017 “clearance operations” constitute genocide and violate the Genocide Convention.

    Industry observers note that bangladesh’s Awami League government, overthrown in 2024, had banned Rohingya children’s access to certified education and higher education in the camps or in the Bangladesh school system. It allowed donor-funded education programs but prohibited Rohingya community-led schools, demolished several, and threatened teachers with exile to Bhasan Char, a remote island.

    The current government has taken positive steps and should lift remaining restrictions on refugees’ access to education amid the donor funding crisis, Human Rights Watch said.

    In October, Bangladesh for the first time allowed a few dozen Rohingya primary students to take an internationally recognized primary school examination, supported by the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

    Also for the first time, Bangladesh in October approved a Rohingya nongovernmental organization’s prepares to build a primary school in the camps for 240 students and to provide a structured curriculum. The Rohingya Centre UK, set up by the diaspora Rohingya community, stated that the 10-subject curriculum will be taught from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., significantly more instruction than students receive in donor-funded education programs. The organization is also running training on the new curriculum for other Rohingya-led schools in the camps.

    It has been revealed that teachers in the camps established the Examination Board of Rohingya Refugees in 2025, which now comprises more than 125 community-led schools with up to 30,000 students, and is working to ensure quality education, including standardized exams in the Myanmar curriculum. Establishing the examination board took a year of volunteer outreach in the camps.

    It has been revealed that however, the Bangladesh government has still not accredited any curriculum for Rohingya children, and because community-led schools lack legal status, they cannot receive foreign support directly. As a result, while the UK organization’s school is able to hire and train Rohingya teachers, the project is formally being implemented through a registered Bangladeshi group. Most community-led schools have to charge students small fees to operate, limiting access, and rely on refugees to donate the use of their small living shelters as makeshift classrooms.

    Eight teachers at community-led schools remarked that to reach more students, they need Bangladesh to grant their schools official status, allow official certification of education and a pathway to higher education, and for the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and humanitarian organizations to acknowledge their work and engage with them.

    A teacher at one of the schools said, “We are spending money to ensure education quality, as if we were a government, but we are not a government, we are simply refugees.” Leaders and teachers offered to collaborate with UNICEF and humanitarian organizations on examinations, quality assurance, and improved teaching.

    Industry observers note that the vast majority of Rohingya students rely on donor-funded humanitarian education programs. Humanitarian groups providing education, coordinated by UNICEF, received just US$29 million from donors towards their 2025 budget request of $72 million, resulting in “learning centers” in the refugee camps closing for months. The education sector laid off teachers, cancelled an early education program, and cut teacher trainings and other programs. In October 2026, a humanitarian education official told Human Rights Watch: “We are struggling to maintain the most basic services. Even textbooks are [insufficient].… We cannot ensure children receive materials like a pencil, a notebook.... Learning centers were damaged by mudslides and climate events, but we do not have funding to carry out repairs.”.

    Sources indicate that several Rohingya instructors at learning centers that rely on humanitarian funds confirmed the lack of resources. A grade 1 instructor said his classroom had no whiteboard, markers, desks, or benches, and students had to share textbooks, pens, and exercise books. A grade 3 instructor worried that “three students are using one set of textbooks.” Rather than teaching one class for the full school day, learning center instructors teach students in two “shifts” per day.

    Recent findings suggest that even after humanitarian agencies reduced their education funding request to $53 million for 2026, donors had pledged only $36 million by mid-October, leaving learning centers at risk of closing again, humanitarian officials said. The World Bank and Education Cannot Wait have provided or pledged funding, but this alone is insufficient. The United States had paid for half the Rohingya education budget before halting its funding in 2025. Globally, humanitarian education funding has fallen by 20 percent since 2023.

    All states are obligated to provide children access to quality education without discrimination, regardless of their refugee status. The Inter-Agency Network for Education in Emergencies’ Minimum Standards emphasize the importance of community leadership and participation in the design and implementation of education programming.

    Industry observers note that “Rohingya children are eager to learn,” noted a Rohingya teacher in the camps. “The problem is that their education has been repeatedly interrupted by circumstances beyond their control. Education needs to be treated as a right, not a temporary humanitarian project.”.

    Sources indicate that the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Afghanistan was created to support efforts to hold the Taliban and others responsible for international crimes in Afghanistan to account. It is expected to include a focus on the Taliban’s crimes against humanity of gender persecution. Like similar mechanisms for Myanmar and Syria, it was designed to collect and preserve evidence and prepare files to support criminal prosecutions. Its formation followed years of campaigning by Afghan and international human rights groups on the basis that it could be a key tool in securing justice for victims of grave abuses. Its investigations could also act as a deterrent for current Taliban commanders.

    In a report prepared for the UN General Assembly’s Fifth Committee, which makes budget decisions, the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions (ACABQ) recommended cutting 7 of 17 posts for 2027 with little explanation – including investigators, legal officers, security personnel, and administrative staff.

    According to recent reports, together with cuts made last year based on its recommendations, implementation of these recommendations would mean cutting by over a third the mechanism’s staffing for 2027, significantly hampering its ability to deliver on its mandate. The cuts would hit particularly hard given the original budget proposal was already scaled back by states negotiating its creation, mindful of the UN financial crisis, as compared to similar mechanisms for Syria and Myanmar.

    Recent findings suggest that the budget advisory committee’s recommendation that the mechanism rely on other parts of the UN for communications, security and administrative support, rather than its own dedicated staff, also risks undermining its independence, a key feature of any criminal probe. The mechanism’s operational independence is intended to ensure the integrity and confidentiality of its work, and security of its staff, witnesses and victims. It is vital given the sensitive nature of its investigations and the risk of political interference.

    According to recent reports, UN member states should reject these proposed cuts and approve the original modest budget requested by the secretary-general — something the General Assembly has done in the past. They should respect the Human Rights Council’s decision and ensure the mechanism can begin its investigations safely, securely and effectively—without further delays.
