    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas answers questions during a visit to the University of Texas at Austin on April 15, 2026. (Photo by Eric Gay/The Associated Press).

    In a recent development, U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas will lead an undergraduate seminar at the University of Texas at Austin on race, equality and political thought in February.

    According to recent reports, the one-credit-hour seminar, “CIV 166 Equality and the New Birth of Freedom,” will include two hours of lecture daily from Feb. 1 to Feb. 5, 2027, for 17 students. Sixty-five applied.

    Students will also meet with Justin Dyer, the dean of the University of Texas at Austin’s School of Civic Leadership, during the seminar, which follows American political thought from the nation’s founding through the Civil War to the present.

    Recent findings suggest that readings include the writings and speeches of Frederick Douglass, Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois, as well as civil rights leaders the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X. The course examines how questions of race and equality show up in recent Supreme Court decisions.

    Thomas previously spoke to students and legal professionals at the University of Texas at Austin in April, making the case that the Supreme Court’s failures have stemmed from a lack of courage, not a lack of understanding, and he discussed Plessy v. Ferguson, a 1896 ruling that upheld government-enforced segregation.

    Thomas, who joined the Supreme Court in 1991, is its longest-serving current member.

    ICC: Afghanistan Decision Risks Narrowing Access to Justice

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that (The Hague) – An International Criminal Court (ICC) decision risks hindering a path to justice for victims of grave crimes committed in Afghanistan, Human Rights Watch stated today.
    • In a recent development, the ICC prosecutor’s office on November 13 sought to appeal the decision and to seek a stay of the closure decision.
    • In a recent development, “Victims of serious international crimes committed by warring parties during Afghanistan’s long conflict have faced many roadblocks to justice,” noted Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that (The Hague) – An International Criminal Court (ICC) decision risks hindering a path to justice for victims of grave crimes committed in Afghanistan, Human Rights Watch stated today. On November 12, 2026, an ICC pretrial chamber, citing a lack of activity, effectively closed the court’s situation dealing with crimes by US, Afghan government, and other forces prior to the Taliban’s August 2021 takeover.

    In a recent development, the ICC prosecutor’s office on November 13 sought to appeal the decision and to seek a stay of the closure decision. Research by Human Rights Watch and others over many years has documented war crimes and crimes against humanity by the Taliban; the Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP), an ISIS-affiliated group; Afghan government forces; and US military and Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) forces.

    In a recent development, “Victims of serious international crimes committed by warring parties during Afghanistan’s long conflict have faced many roadblocks to justice,” noted Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “The ICC judges’ decision threatens to compound barriers to future accountability for US and Afghan government forces.”.

    In its initial 2017 request to open an investigation in Afghanistan, the prosecution cited alleged crimes by US military and CIA forces including torture and cruel treatment, outrages upon personal dignity, and rape and other forms of sexual violence “pursuant to a policy approved by the US authorities.” Regarding Afghan government forces, it cited alleged torture, sexual violence against detainees and civilians, enforced disappearances, and extrajudicial executions.

    With respect to the Taliban’s forces, the crimes included directing attacks on the civilian population and other protected entities, murder, political and gender-based persecution, and the use of child soldiers. During the 20-year conflict, none of the warring parties demonstrated the will to meaningfully deliver justice for crimes committed by their personnel, Human Rights Watch said.

    In March 2020, ICC judges authorized the court’s prosecutor to investigate all alleged crimes falling within the ICC’s jurisdiction in Afghanistan, an ICC member country, since May 1, 2003. The prosecutor was also authorized to investigate crimes if sufficiently linked to the situation and the armed conflict that were committed in the territory of another ICC member country since July 1, 2002. The investigation was paused while the prosecution, and subsequently, the court’s judges considered a request by the then-Afghanistan government to defer ICC proceedings in favor of prosecutions the government asserted it was pursuing. The court’s judges concluded in 2022 that any cases pursued by the former government were at best a “very limited fraction” of those that would be covered by an ICC investigation.

    Since investigations resumed in 2022, the prosecution has indicated it would focus on alleged crimes by the Taliban and the ISKP, while deprioritizing alleged crimes by Afghan security forces and US personnel. In November 2024, in what is known as a state referral, six countries requested the ICC prosecutor to investigate “crimes committed against women and girls after the Taliban takeover in 2021” within the existing investigation. The investigations have yielded four arrest warrants against senior Taliban officials, including its supreme leader, for gender persecution, spotlighting the Taliban’s brutal repression of women, girls, gender non-conforming persons, and their allies.

    Victims and their families, along with Human Rights Watch and other nongovernmental organizations, have criticized the focus on Taliban abuses as creating a double standard, and have repeatedly urged the ICC prosecutor’s office to expand its investigations.

    Earlier in 2026, a pretrial chamber decision in related proceedings led to the separation of the court’s Afghanistan situation—open since 2020—into two different situations, one concerning abuses by Taliban forces since August 2021, and the other covering all other aspects of the originally authorized investigation. The prosecution has appealed in those related proceedings. Only the situation which concerns Taliban abuses, since August 2021, continues under the November 12 closure decision.

    In a recent development, the judges in the November 12 decision relied on a recently adopted court regulation permitting them to close out situation records if the prosecution has provided notice that it had “decide[d] not to initiate an investigation or determine[d] that he or she does not anticipate any further investigatory or prosecutorial activities” in that situation. The prosecution has recently asked the court to close the record in several situations in which it had decided not to initiate an investigation.

    However, the pretrial chamber in this ruling acted on its own initiative. During the proceedings that led to the separation of the Afghanistan situation into two, the prosecution indicated that it was pursuing three lines of inquiry; two concerning alleged Taliban crimes since August 2021, and one concerning alleged ISKP crimes since 2016. The chamber appears to have treated this indication as notification that the prosecution did not intend to pursue other aspects of the originally authorized investigation. It suggested in the closure decision that if the prosecution wished to pursue other lines of inquiry it could request authorization to do so in the future, a process that took more than two years to resolve when the prosecution first sought an Afghanistan investigation in 2017.

    Among other grounds in its appeal, the prosecution claims that it did not provide any notification under this regulation. In the related proceedings, the prosecution had indicated that it did not intend to provide any such notification.

    In a recent development, the court’s decision comes as the ICC faces increasing pressure from the US government, which has vowed to dismantle the court “brick by brick” if necessary to avoid any prosecution of Americans or Israelis. The Trump administration has imposed sanctions on the court that threaten its ability to operate, along with sanctions on several of its judges and prosecutors, three Palestinian human rights organizations, and a UN human rights expert. Human Rights Watch, together with three other organizations, is challenging the sanctions in US federal court.

    Industry observers note that the judges also relied on their own observations that there are “significant limitations to the [p]rosecution’s ability to conduct its investigations and secure evidence,” and that the prosecution had yet to submit arrest warrant applications related to the ISKP. The ICC initially refused to authorize an Afghanistan investigation in 2019, in a decision Human Rights Watch described, at the time, as rewarding obstructionist behavior by states. That decision, overturned by the ICC appeals chamber, was handed down as the court faced hostility by the US government under the first Trump administration.

    Sources indicate that “The ICC acts as a critical court of last resort when other avenues to justice are closed,” Evenson mentioned. “ICC member countries should do all they can to protect the ICC from US attempts to obstruct justice in the cases before it.”.

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that an Azerbaijani court sentenced two activists affiliated with Meclis.info, an independent platform monitoring the country’s parliament, to lengthy prison terms on dubious financial crime charges on November 12, 2026.
    • The Baku Grave Crimes Court sentenced Imran Aliyev, Meclis.info’s co-founder, to 10 years in prison, and Elgiz Gahraman, another co-founder and data analyst, to nine years.
    • According to recent reports, rolled out in 2023, Meclis.info published analyses of Azerbaijan's parliament, scrutinizing lawmakers’ attendance, voting records, and public statements.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that an Azerbaijani court sentenced two activists affiliated with Meclis.info, an independent platform monitoring the country’s parliament, to lengthy prison terms on dubious financial crime charges on November 12, 2026. These are the latest convictions as part of a wider crackdown that has seen scores of journalists, human rights defenders, and civic activists prosecuted on politically motivated charged since late 2023.

    The Baku Grave Crimes Court sentenced Imran Aliyev, Meclis.info’s co-founder, to 10 years in prison, and Elgiz Gahraman, another co-founder and data analyst, to nine years. A third defendant, the platform’s accountant Tamella Musayeva, received a suspended prison sentence. All three were convicted of illegal entrepreneurship, money laundering, currency smuggling, tax evasion, and document forgery.

    According to recent reports, rolled out in 2023, Meclis.info published analyses of Azerbaijan's parliament, scrutinizing lawmakers’ attendance, voting records, and public statements. Aliyev has been in detention since his arrest in April 2024. Gahraman and Musayeva were placed under police supervision in February 2025; Gahraman was taken into custody in the courtroom after the verdict.

    During the trial, Aliyev acknowledged receiving foreign grants, but denied any criminal wrongdoing, maintaining that the prosecution was retaliation for Meclis.info’s work. His lawyer argued that failure to register grants constituted, at most, an administrative offense. Human Rights Watch has documented how Azerbaijani authorities use restrictive legislation and arbitrary registration practices to make it virtually impossible for independent groups to operate and receive foreign funding lawfully.

    Aliyev testified in April that police had beaten him, subjected him to electric shocks, and pressured him to sign documents without a lawyer present following his arrest. The Interior Ministry failed to effectively investigate the allegations.

    Recent findings suggest that this is not Gahraman’s first politically motivated prosecution. Arrested on drug charges in 2016, he was sentenced to prison in 2017 and released by presidential pardon in March 2019. The European Court of Human Rights found in January that his earlier detention had been intended to punish him for his civic and political activism.

    Azerbaijani authorities should immediately release Aliyev, Gahraman, and all others imprisoned on politically motivated charges, overturn the unjust convictions, and end the misuse of foreign funding regulations to silence independent civic groups and media.

    #20736. Court declines to hear dispute tied to George Floyd protests and cases involving former baseball player Roberto Clemente and actor Randy Quaid

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (895 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Court declines to hear dispute tied to George Floyd protests and cases involving former baseball player Roberto Clemente and actor Randy Quaid

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Supreme Court on Monday denied review in over 200 cases, including a dispute that arose in Minneapolis after the murder of George Floyd in police custody in 2020 and clashes involving actor Randy Quaid and the sons of a baseball legend.
    • The court on Friday granted one petition for review from that conference, in a case involving whether and when a bankruptcy court can refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.
    • The Minneapolis case was brought by a group of businesses located at the intersection where Floyd was killed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Supreme Court on Monday denied review in over 200 cases, including a dispute that arose in Minneapolis after the murder of George Floyd in police custody in 2020 and clashes involving actor Randy Quaid and the sons of a baseball legend. These denials were part of a list of orders from the court’s Nov. 6 conference that was released on Monday morning.

    The court on Friday granted one petition for review from that conference, in a case involving whether and when a bankruptcy court can refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.

    The Minneapolis case was brought by a group of businesses located at the intersection where Floyd was killed. Following Floyd’s death, the city blocked the intersection “with concrete barricades,” which “prevented vehicles and pedestrians from accessing” the area, and withdrew police protection, according to the businesses’ petition for review. Those barricades remained in place “for over one year,” and led to significant economic losses for the businesses and a surge in violent crime, the petition said.

    In a recent development, the businesses challenged the city’s actions in state court, alleging that it had violated the Constitution’s takings clause and similar protections in Minnesota’s constitution by interfering with their operations and failing to compensate them accordingly. However, a district court and the Minnesota Court of Appeals disagreed, and the Minnesota Supreme Court denied the businesses’ request for it to review the case.

    Industry observers note that in August, the businesses came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to revive their case. On Monday, the Supreme Court declined to do so without comment.

    In a recent development, the case involving family members of baseball legend Roberto Clemente also involved the takings clause. Clemente’s adult sons and companies associated with preserving Clemente’s legacy challenged Puerto Rico’s use of the baseball legend’s image on “license plates and tags,” an initiative that “generat[ed] 15 million dollars for Puerto Rico” but also fueled ill will against the family, “who Puerto Ricans thought were to blame for a fee levied on them during dire economic times,” according to the petition for review. Through their lawsuit, the Clementes aimed to block Puerto Rico from using their father’s image in the future and recover financial damages.

    Earlier this year, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit prevented the Clemente family’s takings clause claim from proceeding, emphasizing that it (along with the federal statute concerning trademark law) is “designed not to protect legacies but instead to remedy ... the taking of property for public use without just compensation.” In June, the Clementes asked the Supreme Court to take up the case and, among other things, clarify that the takings clause can apply in cases involving intangible property.

    After considering the petition at three consecutive conferences, the justices on Monday denied review.

    In a recent development, the petition for review involving Quaid addressed access to “restricted law-enforcement database material—including criminal history, warrant-status, mug-shot, and jail-record information” – but was perhaps most notable because it was written by Quaid and his wife, Evgenia Quaid. The Quaids contended that “an employee of the Santa Barbara Sheriff’s Department” sent such restricted material concerning the couple to an assistant district attorney, who then sent it to a private attorney, “without subpoena, discovery request, court order, or law-enforcement purpose.” This “unauthorized access” and information sharing violated privacy laws, according to the Quaids.

    They came to the Supreme Court after losing before a federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, which held that the Quaids’ privacy claims “are barred by the litigation privilege,” a legal doctrine that prevents lawsuits over communication that occurs as part of a judicial proceeding. On Monday, the Supreme Court declined to take up the case.

    It has been revealed that in Monday’s order list, the justices also asked the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on AstraZeneca UK Ltd. v. Atchley, a case on whether U.S. terrorism victims may sue 21 “of the world’s largest pharmaceutical and medical-device companies” under the Antiterrorism Act for allegedly aiding and abetting terrorists in Iraq.

    In a recent development, additionally, the justices sent Roybal v. Griffith, a transgender female inmate’s challenge to jail policies in El Paso County, Colorado, regarding the treatment of transgender inmates back to the lower court for reconsideration in light of West Virginia v. B.P.J. and United States v. Skrmetti.

    It has been revealed that in B.P.J., the court ruled in June that state laws barring transgender female athletes from participating on women’s and girls’ sports teams do not violate a federal civil rights law or the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment. In Skrmetti, the court last year upheld a Tennessee law prohibiting some medical treatments for transgender minors, holding that it was not subject to heightened scrutiny under the equal protection clause.

    Also on Monday, the justices granted the solicitor general’s request to participate in three oral arguments during the December argument session:.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    #20734. Supreme Court allows Trump administration to continue border wall construction

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1034 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Supreme Court allows Trump administration to continue border wall construction

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that the Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume construction of a border wall in the Significant Bend region of southwestern Texas.
    • In a recent development, the dispute began earlier this year, when then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued three waivers of various environmental and conservation laws to authorize construction of the wall in the Big Bend region, which includes parts of Big Bend National Park.
    • A group of plaintiffs opposed to the construction – an environmental group, a local landowner who works as a river guide, and a group formed to preserve a church – went to federal court to challenge the waivers’ legality.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume construction of a border wall in the Significant Bend region of southwestern Texas. In a four-page, unsigned opinion, the justices granted the government’s request to pause an order by a federal district judge that had temporarily halted the project. Only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that she would have denied the government’s request.

    In a recent development, the dispute began earlier this year, when then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued three waivers of various environmental and conservation laws to authorize construction of the wall in the Big Bend region, which includes parts of Big Bend National Park. Noem and Mullin relied on a provision of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 that gives the DHS secretary the power to “waive all legal requirements” necessary “to ensure expeditious construction” of border walls and roads. When they unveiled the waivers, Noem and Mullin indicated that the Big Bend area “is an area of high illegal entry” requiring additional walls and barriers.

    A group of plaintiffs opposed to the construction – an environmental group, a local landowner who works as a river guide, and a group formed to preserve a church – went to federal court to challenge the waivers’ legality. On Oct. 2, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone temporarily barred the Department of Homeland Security from continuing construction on the border wall in the Significant Bend region “until and unless” the government complies with environmental and other applicable laws.

    According to recent reports, in a written opinion that she released on Oct. 14, Cardone reasoned that the challengers were likely to prevail on their claim that the DHS secretary did not have the authority to concern the waivers. She relied on the major questions doctrine – the idea that if Congress intends to give a federal agency the power to make decisions of vast economic or political significance, it must say so very clearly. In particular, she emphasized, the Substantial Bend region is not an area with a high number of illegal entries. To the contrary, she stated, although it “comprises over 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border,” it makes up only a tiny percentage (“between 0.3% and 2.2%”) of the migrants apprehended while crossing the border. Therefore, she wrote, “if the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector, and the waiver authority would apply to the entire U.S.-Mexico border. If that were the case, Congress could have simply authorized construction ‘to deter illegal crossings.’” The major questions doctrine instructs courts to avoid “interpretations that would render limiting language meaningless,” Cardone concluded.

    After Cardone declined to pause her ruling to give the government time to seek Supreme Court review, the Trump administration came to the Supreme Court, where it asked the justices not only to temporarily freeze Cardone’s order but also to grant review and summarily (that is, without additional briefing or oral argument) reverse it. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued that Cardone lacked the power to consider the challengers’ claim based on the major questions doctrine because their complaint specifically alleged that the DHS secretary “lacked ‘clear congressional authorization’ … to problem the waivers” under the IIRIRA – which, he said, was a statutory claim that “Congress denied district courts” the authority “to entertain.” But in any event, Sauer continued, even if the DHS secretary’s power to issue waivers under IIRIRA “implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the Secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction.”.

    Industry observers note that the challengers urged the justices to leave Cardone’s order in place. Eric Glitzenstein, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs, told the justices in a 40-page filing that if her order were paused or lifted, it would permit the Trump administration to “immediately resume blasting, bulldozing, road construction, and other border barrier-related construction across one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally significant landscapes in the United States.”.

    Sources indicate that the challengers argued that the major questions doctrine applied to their claim. They emphasized that the DHS secretary’s “decision to waive myriad federal, state, local, and tribal laws across vast geography for the purpose of building border infrastructure, even through national and state parks where border crossings are miniscule, is a truly ‘extraordinary’ assertion of power.” Because Congress “did not clearly authorize the sweeping exercise of power asserted here,” they wrote, the government’s “actions therefore amount to a constitutional violation of the major questions doctrine.”.

    In Monday’s opinion, the justices denied the government’s request to summarily reverse Cardone’s ruling but granted its request to put it on hold. “The Government,” the court explained, “is exceedingly likely to prevail on its argument” that Cardone did not have the power to consider the challengers’ “so-called major-questions-doctrine claim.” That claim, the court emphasized, contends only “that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority,” which is not a constitutional claim. This is true, the court continued, even if the challengers rely on the major-questions doctrine, because that doctrine is a rule used to interpret laws. “There is no such thing as a ‘constitutional’ major-questions claim.”.

    The other factors that courts normally consider in deciding whether to pause a lower court’s decision also point in the government’s favor, the justices said. For example, Cardone’s order “delays the Government’s construction of border barriers and roads in the Big Bend Sector” and, as a result, “impedes the Government from advancing its ‘compelling interests’ in border security and integrity.” Moreover, the government is suffering permanent harm from the costs – “nearly half a million dollars … per day” – that it is incurring while the construction is on hold, but which cannot be recovered. Finally, the court wrote, “[t]he Government’s interest … outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by” the challengers.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, calling a judge a vulgar name is rude, but it does not amount to criminal contempt, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court recently found. (Image from Shutterstock).

    The criminal contempt conviction of a courtroom spectator who called a judge a vulgar name after she ruled against a motion that his acquaintance filed was recently vacated by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court.

    According to recent reports, basile Outlaw spent 30 days in jail after the 2022 incident involving Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas Judge Roxanne E. Covington, Reason reports.

    “What did you say?” Covington responded to his remark, according to the article.

    “Never mind, I’m leaving,” Outlaw said.

    He claims that he later came back to apologize and was taken into custody, Reason reports.

    It has been revealed that in December 2023, the Pennsylvania Superior Court upheld Outlaw’s conviction. The state supreme court reversed and vacated the conviction in late October, finding that while what Outlaw did was rude, it wasn’t enough for criminal contempt.

    The majority opinion cited an earlier finding involving a pro se party in a custody dispute calling the judge a vulgar term.

    Here, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court also reversed a criminal contempt conviction for the party. In both cases, the state supreme court found, the outbursts amounted to momentary breaks in the proceedings, not significant disruptions.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It was a busy Monday at the Supreme Court: the justices heard two oral arguments, released an order list, and decided the border wall dispute on the interim docket. Keep reading to catch up on these and other developments.

    On Monday, the Supreme Court granted the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to resume construction of its border wall in the Major Bend region of southwestern Texas. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that she would deny the request. Learn more about the dispute in the On Site section below.

    Sources indicate that earlier on Monday, the justices heard arguments in two cases: Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations; and Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires.

    Also on Monday, the Supreme Court denied review in over 200 cases, including disputes involving the George Floyd protests in Minneapolis, actor Randy Quaid, and the sons of former baseball player Roberto Clemente. It also asked the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a case over whether U.S. terrorism victims may sue 21 pharmaceutical and medical-device companies under the Antiterrorism Act for allegedly aiding and abetting Iraqi terrorists. For more on Monday’s order list, see the On Site section.

    Today, the justices will hear argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC, on whether the Constitution allows the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – to adjudicate an employer’s obligation to comply with employment agreements concerning temporary immigrant workers.

    On Wednesday, the Supreme Court Building will be closed in recognition of Veterans Day.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that listen up, wiseguys. There’s a fresh Disney/Pixar movie coming out, and it’s a crime movie! Specifically, it’s a movie about the Italian mob. It takes place in Venice, Italy, and is the story of a scrawny, impoverished young fellow named Nero (voiced by Mark Ruffalo) who is taken in by a powerful crime family. In exchange for this, his job is to steal things for them… often at great personal risk.

    Also, they’re all cats. Everybody’s a cat. Well, a couple of characters seem to be rodents. And there’s a pigeon, I think. But it’s mostly cats. The film is titled Gatto (which is Italian for “cat”).

    Anyway, Nero starts to find himself in very dangerous situations, working as a thief for the (literal) fat cat crime boss Rocco, and learns that he has nine lives that he’s wasting, dying while doing criminal errands. Thus, he asks himself the great questions many crime movie protagonists ask themselves: is everything he’s doing worth it? Is he living a life that’s worth living as if it’s his only one? How can he change his life so that it’s full of meaning?

    In addition to Ruffalo, the voice cast includes: Laurence Fishburne, Enrico Casarosa (who also directs), John Turturro, Isabella Rossellini, Natasia Demetriou, Jamie Demetriou, Jason Schwartzman, Saverio Raimondo, Jason Mantzoukas, Tracey Ullman, Marco Calvani, and Rhys Darby.

    Recent findings suggest that perhaps it’s a great film to take your children to as you start to introduce them to the “mafia movie” genre. Watch Gatto and then The Godfather and find out which one they like better!

    According to recent reports, the film will be in theaters next March. Ci vediamo!

    #20729. Justices dubious of fee award in eminent domain dispute about interstate pipeline

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (794 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Justices dubious of fee award in eminent domain dispute about interstate pipeline

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The argument yesterday in Hoffmann v.
    • The dispute involves the 1947 Natural Gas Act’s treatment of interstate natural-gas pipelines.
    • The landowners here argue, with some support in the lower courts, that if the pipeline manufacturer rather than the United States condemns the land, the pipeline company should be bound by state-law rules that require more compensation than the federal Constitution.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The argument yesterday in Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc. left little doubt about how the justices will resolve this one: they seem unlikely to hold that the gas company condemning land for a federally approved pipeline should have to pay attorneys’ fees that the United States would not have to pay if it condemned the land directly.

    The dispute involves the 1947 Natural Gas Act’s treatment of interstate natural-gas pipelines. When the federal government approves such a pipeline, the Natural Gas Act allows it to acquire the land in which to build the pipeline or leave that to the gas tech giant. In either case, if the landowner does not agree, a suit exercising the federal government’s right of eminent domain can force a transfer of the land for a “necessary right-of-way,” so long as the landowner receives the “just compensation” that the Fifth Amendment requires when property is “taken for public use.”.

    The landowners here argue, with some support in the lower courts, that if the pipeline manufacturer rather than the United States condemns the land, the pipeline company should be bound by state-law rules that require more compensation than the federal Constitution. In particular, North Dakota law well might require the company to pay the attorneys’ fees of the landowners.

    Industry observers note that the justices, though, were having none of it. The air was redolent with skepticism from the moment Robert McNamara rose to press the landowners’ view. Justice Clarence Thomas started off by asking – doubtfully – whether “if the U.S. delegates its power … of eminent domain, you’re saying that it brings with it state law trappings of just compensation?” Chief Justice John Roberts quickly interjected that “it seems to me it’s just a more efficient process to have a private developer get the land under the same terms as the federal government without having to pay the attorneys’ fees that the state wants to insist on.” When McNamara stuck to his position, the chief justice eventually concluded the discussion by commenting: “I don’t understand why this isn’t an easy case.”.

    It seemed for a while that several of the justices would offer a slightly different reason to reject McNamara’s argument, with Justice Sonia Sotomayor coming in quickly to press the idea that “you’re trying to separate the right to eminent domain from the right to compensation, correct?” and then pointing to “a[n] 1893 case … in which we said, [it is] a settled principle of universal law that [they are] inseparably connected. … I don’t see how your separation of these principles honors that.”.

    Industry observers note that for Ketanji Brown Jackson, the problem was McNamara’s assumption “that state law, with respect to just compensation is the default,” and that “it needed to be ousted by congressional expression.” But if that were true, she pointed out, why would Congress have thought it important, in a 1946 condemnation statute adopted just one year before the Natural Gas Act, to take the trouble explicitly to import state law? That statute’s treatment of the condemnation problem appears to contrast sharply with the treatment in the Natural Gas Act just one year later. As Jackson asked pointedly: “What is [that language] doing there if … silence [by Congress means that] state law applies?” Justices Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett pressed McNamara on the same point: they took it as self-evident that the 1946 statute importing state law suggested that a 1947 statute silent on the topic calls for the application of the baseline federal rule emphasized by Thomas and Roberts.

    You have to expect it will be pretty hard to fashion a majority if Justice Thomas and the chief justice on one side see it as an “easy case” against you and Jackson and Sotomayor on the other side are predisposed to reject what you have to say. And nothing in the remainder of the argument suggested any reason to think otherwise. The presentations of Paul Hughes (for the pipeline firm) and Zoe Jacoby (for the government) were filled for the most part with softball questions speculating about why lower courts might have found such an obvious question challenging.

    Sources indicate that I would not be at all surprised if this was one of the very first decisions from the November session. The share of simple unanimous statutory cases is not so high as it used to be, but this has all the earmarks of a straightforward unanimous affirmance.

    Ronald Mann is a professor of law at Columbia, where he teaches courses in commercial finance, payment systems and deals.

    #20728. Industry News: 7 idiosyncratic novels that leave Laurie Cass in awe

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (968 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: 7 idiosyncratic novels that leave Laurie Cass in awe

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (968 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When I came up with the topic for this post, I thought it would be the work of a few minutes to come up with half a dozen titles, parse out reasons why each one was included in the list, and conclude with a clever sentence or two.
    • What actually happened was I stared at my computer screen for an absurd amount of time, typing and deleting, typing and deleting.
    • Sources indicate that the end result is, in retrospect, overwhelmingly obvious: I could never write a book that isn’t mine to write.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When I came up with the topic for this post, I thought it would be the work of a few minutes to come up with half a dozen titles, parse out reasons why each one was included in the list, and conclude with a clever sentence or two.

    What actually happened was I stared at my computer screen for an absurd amount of time, typing and deleting, typing and deleting. When it became clear that I wasn’t getting anywhere, I got up and wandered over to my bookshelves and sat down in front of them to have a good long think.

    Sources indicate that the end result is, in retrospect, overwhelmingly obvious: I could never write a book that isn’t mine to write. Discovering what’s in you that can become a book is part of the joy of writing, and what an author brings to a manuscript is what makes it theirs and theirs alone.

    That noted, there are books—and entire genres—that will forever be out of my authorial reach.

    Sources indicate that let’s start with one of my favorite books, Dissolution by C. J. Sansom. The main character of Matthew Shardlake is deeply complex, and his complicated history and personality twist together around and into the intricate plot. It’s set in 1537 England, during the reign of King Henry VIII, a period rife with fear and conflict.

    There is no way on this good green earth that I could write a book with anything remotely similar to the complexity of Dissolution. Not the tiniest sliver of a chance. If I didn’t have the same thing for breakfast every weekday, I wouldn’t remember what I had for breakfast; writing a book with so many layers is not something my brain is likely to take kindly to doing.

    Recent findings suggest that and then there’s the research factor. Serious amounts of time are required to immerse yourself in the zillions of details it takes to write historicals. I love learning things, but until I retire from my day job, doing in-depth research is not in the cards.

    Miles Franklin, My Brilliant Career.

    According to recent reports, next on the list is My Brilliant Career by Miles Franklin. To write like that? As a teenager? Please. My teenaged writing output was embarrassingly bad poetry that is long lost to the mists of time, exactly where it belongs. Ms. Franklin’s talents were, and are, beyond mine. No way, no how, could I have written that.

    Another one on the Beyond Me list has to be The Book Thief by Markus Zusak. A story narrated by Death? That I might be able to write, but a story as bone-deep sad as The Book Thief isn’t something I feel capable of doing. When writing, I tend to inhabit the heads of my main characters, and spending that much time in sorrow, sadness, and despair, would not be good for me on any level.

    I admire those who can do so and walk away intact, but  writing that intense is far outside my capacities.

    Alexander Dumas, The Count of Monte Cristo.

    I read this book for the first time as a teenager, and I flat out loved it. Reread it numerous times, and then put it away when I went off to college.

    Sources indicate that when I picked it up a few years ago, I still enjoyed the read and still feel it’s a quality book, but I noticed something I hadn’t as a youngster: there’s nothing funny in it. Not a word. The only things I can write don’t include humor are professional white papers and reports. And it’s possible that funny bits sneak into those, every so often. Writing a full-length novel with a total of no humor is not going to happen.

    Recent findings suggest that E. L. James, Fifty Shades of Grey.

    Industry observers note that I included this on my Couldn’t Write list because of its reputation for explicit sex scenes. There are many, many other books that contain the act, and I don’t see how I could have written any of them. In what I write, all that happens off-book, if it happens at all. Fade to black at end of chapter works for me, and until an editor tells me differently, that’s how it’s going to stay.

    I read this book in one sitting. Or more accurately, since I was in a hammock at the time, in one lying, but the point remains. I did not want to do *anything* until I found out what happened. The characters, the pacing, the stakes, the stark wonder of the discoveries—maybe I could wrap one of those elements into a book, two if I was lucky, but all of them together? Nope. That high-concept stuff is way outside my abilities.

    Plus there’s the science element. I’m geeky by nature, but the time spent researching would be a massive barrier, similar to the above-mentioned historical research.

    Helene Hanff, 84, Charing Cross Road.

    Recent findings suggest that this book. This. Book. It captured my heart when I first read it decades ago, and it could well be what started me on a lifelong love affair with London. I don’t know what makes it such a lovely, lovely book; the lyrical quality of the correspondence? The gaps left to the reader to fill? The bittersweet tone you can almost taste?

    I’m not sure, and it now occurs to me that I haven’t reread 84, Charing Cross Road in years. That whisper I hear, is it calling my name? Why, yes, I think it is. Excuse me, but I have to go.

    Laurie Cass is the national bestselling author of the Bookmobile Cat Mystery series.

    #20727. Tech Report: How true crime both mesmerizes and misleads audiences

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1709 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: How true crime both mesmerizes and misleads audiences

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that I had the honor of serving as a Criminal Profiler for more than a decade of the twenty-two years I spent as an FBI Special Agent.
    • Industry observers note that then, as an FBI Agent, I investigated bank robberies, white collar crimes, civil rights violations, child sex crimes, serial murder and rape, child abductions, and terrorism.
    • In the DC Sniper case, for example, I witnessed firsthand what it was like to know that anyone could be shot dead, at any place, at any time, in the greater DC area.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that I had the honor of serving as a Criminal Profiler for more than a decade of the twenty-two years I spent as an FBI Special Agent. Before the FBI, I was a prosecutor for the New York City Law Department. While there, I tried cases from petty theft to sex crimes and extortion to attempted murder.

    Industry observers note that then, as an FBI Agent, I investigated bank robberies, white collar crimes, civil rights violations, child sex crimes, serial murder and rape, child abductions, and terrorism. I traveled across the country and around the world chasing the worst of the worst that humanity has to offer. Some of those offenders were among the most notorious criminals of our time.

    In the DC Sniper case, for example, I witnessed firsthand what it was like to know that anyone could be shot dead, at any place, at any time, in the greater DC area. That’s because people were being killed right in my own backyard.

    It has been revealed that from the start that case presented differently from other “spree killer” cases. Typically in spree cases, as the offender moves from shooting scene to shooting scene he decompensates and his criminal sophistication erodes. In other words, his crimes become more and more sloppy.

    But here, the shooter made one shot/one kill, six times in a row while moving from location to location in rapid succession and no one ever even saw him. He was a ghost….

    Recent findings suggest that fortunately, though, his behavior leaked out enough information that we were able to build a profile of not one, but two snipers, working together for the first time in US history. One older with police or military training and experience, and the other a teen who had written the communications on a tarot card and on children’s note paper. In the end, shortly after our profile was released, the snipers were spotted by an alert trucker who immediately called 911 and ended their twenty-three-day reign of terror.

    Another notorious case involved JonBenét Ramsey, a six-year-old beauty pageant queen—who was reportedly kidnapped but was later found dead in the basement of her home. The case still remains officially unsolved decades later.

    In my opinion, this is not due to law enforcement incompetence, but because the family refused to be fully interviewed by law enforcement for several months, the father filed multiple law suits against investigators, and the prosecutor made a decision not to follow through with the murder indictments voted for by the grand jury.

    Industry observers note that in 2009, when I retired from the FBI and transitioned into full-time network television writing and producing, it was only natural that I gravitate toward what I knew best—crime. I formed a development and production organization, XG Productions, with my brother Tim, also a retired FBI agent. Together, we endeavor to put crime victims first (not notorious offenders) and bring authenticity to the crime entertainment space.

    It has been revealed that one of the most successful shows I worked on as a writer/producer was the popular ABC/CBS prime time crime drama, Criminal Minds. In fact, we just finished shooting our nineteenth season at the time of this writing. I also worked on FBI, FBI Most Wanted, Blind Spot, Sleepy Hollow, Quantico, and many more. And XG also produced The Case Of: JonBenét Ramsey, The Case Of: Caylee Anthony, The Forgotten West Memphis Three, and INDIVISIBLE: Healing Hate.

    Recent findings suggest that I published my first true crime book, Without Consent, in 2014. And since 2020, XG Productions has produced and published twenty-five Audible Original Docuseries. These include: Evil Has A Name, Paul Holes’ story of his relentless pursuit and identification of the Golden State Killer, with the help of the FBI’s Steve Kramer and Steve Busch. In the process of solving this decades-old cold case, they created Forensic Genetic Genealogy—a monumental breakthrough that has changed law enforcement forever.

    Recent findings suggest that where The Devil Belongs is the story of the most prolific serial bomber in US history, The Unabomber. And Call Me God, is the story of the DC Snipers. All of these titles are based on cases my colleagues at the BAU and I actually investigated and analyzed.

    Sources indicate that in 2024, I also co-wrote and produced my bestselling audio drama, Bluebeard, starring Joseph Fiennes, Karen David, Holt McCallany, and Adrian Pasdar. Bluebeard is closely based on the true story of Los Angeles’s first serial killer, James “Bluebeard” Watson, who married thirty women and killed more than a dozen of them.

    I’m pretty sure everyone reading this introduction has noticed the rapid expansion of true crime across all forms of media in recent years. In fact, the proliferation of true crime over the last decade has been nothing short of phenomenal.

    In a recent development, during that time, I was fortunate enough to launch a couple of successful podcasts. The first, Real Crime Profile—in which my FBI Profiler colleague, Kathy Canning-Mello and I discuss and analyze current and historical criminal cases from a behavioral perspective. Then about a year later we launched Best Case Worst Case, in which my colleague and fellow FBI Agent Maureen O’Connell and I interview law enforcement professionals about the best and worst cases of their careers.

    Over a hundred million downloads later, I’ve enjoyed educating listeners while they are being entertained. I’ve also noticed a concerning trend, though. People have asked why I chose the name “Real” Crime Profile instead of what might have been a more popular moniker, “True” Crime Profile.

    In a recent development, the choice was intentional. The popularity of “True Crime” across all platforms has given rise to a number of podcasts, docudramas, fictional series, and, frankly, Tik-Tok and Instagram posts, with hosts that “love” True Crime but know absolutely nothing about real crime and actual criminal investigations.

    Industry observers note that as a result, there are millions of listeners and viewers who are being misinformed and misled. Were it just for entertainment purposes, that might not be so bad. But that’s not the case. People actually believe a great deal of what they see and hear on TV, podcasts, and social media. Fortunately, the best true crime show runners, writers, and producers hire law enforcement professionals as tech advisors and/or writers—because they care enough to get it right.

    In a recent development, A great example of this happened early in my writing career. It started while I was still in the Behavioral Analysis Unit, when we conducted a study on child abduction homicides in the US. Over the next decade I taught about 60,000 law enforcement professionals, citing the results of that study.

    Later, I wrote my first scene of Criminal Minds, in which Dr. Reid spouts off those statistics as he magically morphs on screen into a playground with ten children happily running around. As he says, “Of those children who are abducted and killed, forty-four percent die within the first hour,” half of the kids on the playground disappear. “[S]eventy-three percent in the first three hours,” and three-quarters of the kids are gone.

    Then there is one little girl left swinging on a swing as he states, “And ninety-nine percent in the first twenty-four hours,” and the girl disappears, leaving the swing, swinging back and forth…empty.

    When I saw that scene on TV the hair immediately stood up on the back of my neck. It also caused a “fight or flight” reaction in me and I had to get up and walk around the room to burn off the excess energy. I was overwhelmed with the visual depiction of statistics I had repeated hundreds of times in person. That’s because I realized that in under two minutes I had just reached over 17 million people. And by the time that episode went through syndication, 163 million people saw it and were now educated about the urgency surrounding child abductions. Media is a huge force multiplier and I was hooked.

    Industry observers note that as a profiler, people have often asked me what I think about the explosion of true crime entertainment and social media and the fact that up to eighty-five percent of the audience is made up of women. Many people think it is a result of a sick fascination with the macabre.

    I have a very different view. I believe that since women are caring, nurturing, and protective by nature, they are drawn to true crime because they want to learn how bad things happen. This is so they can use that information to protect those they love. It’s the same principal that almost forces us to “rubberneck” as we pass by accidents on the road. We feel a very strong pull to see what happened to the people in the accident, so we can avoid having the same thing happen to us.

    This is not a negative personality trait. It is an instinctual and effective survival mechanism.

    Industry observers note that as you read the [stories in The Best True Crime Stories of the Year 2026], keep this in mind. If you want to get the most out of true crime, you might want to pay more attention to the professionals who are trained and experienced in investigating and prosecuting real criminals.

    Industry observers note that retired FBI Supervisory Special Agent (SSA) Jim Clemente was a member of the National Center for the Analysis of Violent Crime, an integral part of the FBI's Critical Incident Response Group. During his prosecutive and investigative careers, Clemente investigated hundreds of cases involving the sexual victimization of children and has consulted and assisted in the investigation and prosecution of thousands more. Since his retirement from the FBI, Clemente has served as co-founder and board Chair of XG Productions, Inc. He has also served as inspiration for and Writer/Producer of, one of Television’s longest running prime time dramatic series, Criminal Minds. His audiobook, Bluebeard, based on real events surrounding Los Angeles’s first known serial killer received rave reviews following its 2023 release. He is also the editor of The Best True Crime Stories of the Year 2026.

    #20725. Trump administration brings White House ballroom battle back to Supreme Court

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1194 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump administration brings White House ballroom battle back to Supreme Court

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1194 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court last week, once again asking the justices to intervene in its ongoing efforts to build a latest White House ballroom.
    • Construction on the project began in October of last year with the demolition of the East Wing.
    • To support its argument that it had a legal right to sue, known as standing, the trust submitted a declaration from Alison Hoagland, a member who lives in Washington, D.C., and stated that she visits the area where the White House is located approximately once per month.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court last week, once again asking the justices to intervene in its ongoing efforts to build a latest White House ballroom. On Aug. 31, a divided court paused a ruling by a federal judge in Washington, D.C., that would have halted above-ground construction on the project. In a petition filed on Nov. 5, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the court to reverse the lower court’s ruling outright or to take up the case and hear oral arguments on the merits. He told the justices that their earlier ruling “has all but answered the question presented” by the dispute, and that the project “should be permitted to move forward outside the shadow of judicial superintendence.”.

    Construction on the project began in October of last year with the demolition of the East Wing. In December, the National Trust for Historic Preservation – a private nonprofit that describes itself as having “led the movement to save America’s historic places” “[f]or more than 75 years” – filed a lawsuit in federal court, seeking to block the construction until the National Capital Planning Commission and the Commission of Fine Arts could review the aims for the construction; the NCPC could approve those plans; and Congress could authorize the construction.

    To support its argument that it had a legal right to sue, known as standing, the trust submitted a declaration from Alison Hoagland, a member who lives in Washington, D.C., and stated that she visits the area where the White House is located approximately once per month. Hoagland, who has “expertise in historic architecture,” claimed that the project caused “‘injuries’ to her ‘aesthetic, cultural, and historical interests’ because she finds the ‘scale,’ ‘height,’ and ‘massing’ of the government’s design distasteful.”.

    Sources indicate that senior U.S. District Judge Leon issued an order in late March that temporarily barred the construction of the ballroom above ground but allowed underground construction – of, for example, bomb shelters and bunkers – to move forward, along with any above-ground construction necessary for safety and security.

    Before Leon’s ruling could go into effect, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit froze it to give that court time to consider the government’s appeal. In August, a divided three-judge panel of the D.C. Circuit upheld Leon’s ruling but delayed its effective date for 14 days to allow the federal government to go to the Supreme Court.

    Writing for the majority, Judges Patricia Millett and Bradley Garcia emphasized that Congress, and only Congress, has the power “to regulate the construction and demolition of White House structures,” but it has not approved any money for the ballroom construction.

    In her dissent, Judge Neomi Rao contended (among other things) that the trust did not have a legal right to bring a lawsuit, known as standing, to try to stop the ballroom construction.

    Calling Leon’s ruling “extraordinary and unlawful,” the Trump administration came to the court on its interim docket on Aug. 13. Sauer asked the justices to temporarily pause Leon’s ruling, telling them that it would “halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security.” He argued that the trust lacks standing to sue, because its claims rest on a member’s “dislike” for the new construction – which, it mentioned, is not the kind of injury that would allow the lawsuit to go forward.

    It has been revealed that on Aug. 21, the day that Leon’s order was scheduled to go into effect, Chief Justice John Roberts issued an administrative stay – that is, an order that kept Leon’s order on hold (and permitted construction to continue) – to give the justices additional time to consider the government’s request.

    By a vote of 5-4, the court on Aug. 31 granted the government’s application and continued the pause on Leon’s order. In an eight-page, unsigned opinion, the majority stressed that it was not deciding whether the project was legal. Instead, it noted, the trust likely lacks standing to challenge the project at all. The harms that Hoagland alleges, the majority wrote, are not the kind of “concrete” and specific injuries required to bring a lawsuit. Moreover, the majority said, if Leon’s order were allowed to go into effect, the government would be permanently harmed – another key criterion in determining whether to grant emergency relief. Among other things, it noted, senior government officials “attest[] that constructing something approximating the height and mass of the intended above-ground ballroom is ‘crucial’ to the security of the below-ground military installation.”.

    Sources indicate that roberts dissented, in an opinion joined by Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson. In his view, the construction “is likely unlawful,” and the majority’s decision was “no victory for the separation of powers.” He contended that the trust did have standing to sue because “[a] historic preservationist such as Hoagland can be aesthetically injured in a concrete, particularized way by the transformation of a historic building that she frequently enjoys, just as,” based on prior court precedent, “an environmentalist can sustain a concrete, particularized aesthetic injury from the extinction of a particular animal or the transformation of a particular forest or river that he regularly enjoys.”.

    In a recent development, in its Nov. 5 petition, the Trump administration argued that “the East Wing renovation is a vital national-security effort taking place on the White House grounds with the President’s personal involvement,” and that it has “proceeded swiftly since construction began in October 2025, in keeping with the urgency of remedying the East Wing’s obsolete and vulnerable security infrastructure, all as this President faces an onslaught of assassination attempts.” Because Leon’s order blocked the project “at the behest of a single passerby who complains that she expects to dislike its ultimate design,” Sauer wrote, his “decision is demonstrably flawed.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sauer acknowledged that the court’s Aug. 31 ruling came on the interim docket and therefore “only involve[d] a preliminary look at the merits and equities” of the dispute. But, he continued, in this case “[t]here is nothing further or upcoming that this Court needs to decide after its” earlier opinion “in order to answer the question presented” by the government’s new filing – specifically, whether Leon was wrong to block “the ongoing renovation of the East Wing of the White House.” This is especially true, Sauer suggested, given the court made its Aug. 31 decision “after extensive briefing, and problem[d] detailed majority and dissenting opinions addressing” the concerns in the case.

    Sauer urged the court to summarily reverse Leon’s decision – that is, to reverse it without additional briefing or oral argument – or, at a minimum, grant review and hear oral arguments.

    In a recent development, the trust’s response to the government’s petition is right now due on Dec. 7.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    #20724. Andrew H. Murray on thrillers, the Booker, and taking comedy seriously in literature

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1273 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Andrew H. Murray on thrillers, the Booker, and taking comedy seriously in literature

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The UK has just recovered from Booker Prize Fever—alright, not so much a fever as a very, very slightly raised temperature–but in the last week there was a fair bit of interest in this massive and prestigious book award, mainly because the winner’s sales always go right to the moon.
    • My favorite of the books on the shortlist and the one I hoped would win was the terrific Black Bag.
    • I wanted Black Bag to win because I myself make my books funny as well as serious—I can’t help it—and my characters have senses of humor.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The UK has just recovered from Booker Prize Fever—alright, not so much a fever as a very, very slightly raised temperature–but in the last week there was a fair bit of interest in this massive and prestigious book award, mainly because the winner’s sales always go right to the moon.

    My favorite of the books on the shortlist and the one I hoped would win was the terrific Black Bag. It’s a mad story about a young out-of-work actor who is paid to wear a huge black bag and attend university lectures as part of a psychological experiment. Things rapidly get very weird; it’s a very funny book. But when awards night rolled around, in my opinion the jokes in it were far likelier to kneecap its chances than to help it over the line.

    I wanted Black Bag to win because I myself make my books funny as well as serious—I can’t help it—and my characters have senses of humor. My newly introduced book, Everything Happens So Much, is a story about why life feels so strange and difficult, and about why we’re all spending our one wonderful life comparing ourselves to strangers online who are supposedly having much better lives than us.

    Sources indicate that the main character of Everything Happens So Much, Esme, goes to hell and back. She’s put through the wringer. And yet, despite all the Deep Trauma she undergoes, the story has jokes in it, and the jokes are some of the bits I’m proudest of.

    No matter. Across the board in mainstream culture, there is a feeling that if you put jokes in, you can’t possibly do the serious stuff as well. Comedy indicates are written off as trivial, lightweight, split off into their own genre at the non-award-winning end of the room. When did a really funny film last win Best Picture?

    Recent findings suggest that as a result, many writers who do comedy but aspire to mainstream success try to hide the fact. Black Bag has been sold on its chin-stroking lessons about masculinity, rather than its very good one-liners about life as an unemployed actor.

    Another of my other favorite authors right now writing is Mick Herron, author of the terrific Slough House set of thrillers. The Slough House books are set in a crew of failed spies, the agents who’ve wrecked their careers by leaving a secret document on the bus or screwing up a training exercise or simply being too unpleasant to work with.

    Sources indicate that in the hands of an unfunny author the books could have been an unremitting trudge through concrete canyons under grey skies. But Herron, and his characters, are funny. They are biting and cynical and everyone talks like they’ve been written for Apple TV. It’s not unconnected to this that they have been turned into umpteen series for Apple TV.

    And is this comedy element of the books made obvious to the casual viewer? It is not. The covers are serious, the straplines are serious, they’re sold on their thrills. There aren’t many blurbs from other authors about how hilarious the books are. But when you read them, as well as being swept along by the plots, you laugh.

    In my own case, I can’t help it. I started out writing for QI, the British panel show, where the aim is to tell people the most interesting facts in the funniest possible way. The whole show is an exercise in ‘education by stealth’, on the principle that if you’re laughing, you won’t realize you’re learning.

    I then cofounded the podcast No Such Thing As A Fish, which has the same aim. I write for Private Eye magazine—imagine The Onion, but topical. I’m well aware of what you have to do to sell a book these days, though, and it’s this: lie your head off about whether you’re trying to be funny.

    Why is there this snootiness towards comedy? In my view comedy is much harder to write than the serious stuff. Pathos is simply a matter of making things sadder, which any fool can manage. Just give Tiny Tim one more disease or make Anna Karenina’s life that smidge worse: instant tragedy!

    According to recent reports, what’s hard is doing a good tight one-paragraph about life as a nineteenth-century serf which will have your reader laughing until they can’t breathe. (This, incidentally, is why Tolstoy was never given his own HBO special.).

    But the myth persists that funny can’t coexist along with serious, despite all the evidence from our lives that it is in the most serious moments that we are most in need of our senses of humor. When I talk about Everything Happens So Much—to remind you, my new book which is available now—even I fall prey to this terrible effect.

    Industry observers note that I shouldn’t even be admitting this to you. I should be amping up the elements of existential angst. But, honestly, the book contains jokes interwoven with the existential angst, and there’s nothing I can do about it.

    In a recent development, maybe this defensiveness about comedy in most media is because everyone is aware that it yields rewards. Comedians sell out stadiums, they get specials, the clips of their crowd work or their sketches absolutely saturate most media. Why the hell should they have the book market stitched up too?

    But I think the real reason is that jokes are binary—you either get them or you don’t—and the truth is that it’s almost impossible to write a book which will appeal to everyone. All our lives are different, and so all the things we laugh at will be slightly different too. We can all agree that the ending of Of Mice And Men is a tearjerker; if it had ended with Lenny and George doing a tight five at a local comedy club, only about half the readership would have found it funny.

    It has been revealed that the real truth, though, is that funny is the caramel which only heightens the salt. We live in this world, with all its absurdities and tragedies, and yet we know that life is a comedy even if sometimes we watch it through tears. Comedy and tragedy prop each other up and help each other towards the finish line. A novel of pure comedy would be far too light; a purely tragic novel would be too grim to finish. (Thomas Hardy, I’m looking at you.).

    Sources indicate that so if you yourself write funny, if you can’t help it, if a sense of humor keeps breaking out despite your best intentions, then for goodness’ sake embrace it. Know and appreciate your amazing power.

    Recent findings suggest that but my only advice is this: don’t let on. And don’t, whatever you do, write an entire article confessing your upcoming book, which is available now, is extremely funny as well as poignant and thought-provoking. It will do sales no good whatsoever.

    Everything Happens So Much is available to buy now.

    It has been revealed that andrew H. Murray is an author, broadcaster and comedian. He cohosts the award-winning podcast No Such Thing As a Fish, which is one of the top 10 podcasts in the UK and has been downloaded 500 million times, as well as BBC Radio 4's satirical news program The Naked Week. He writes jokes and journalism for Private Eye (think: a hybrid of The Onion and The Nation). He is the author of Everything Happens So Much. Murray lives in London.
